MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ review: RTX Spark power comes to Windows on Arm desktops, but there are trade-offs

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3372 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, MSI's EdgeMesa N AI+ mini PC brings Nvidia RTX Spark power to a Windows on Arm desktop.
  • Solid local AI performance for LLMs and image generation, as expected.
  • Familiar Windows 11 user experience and app compatibility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, MSI's EdgeMesa N AI+ mini PC brings Nvidia RTX Spark power to a Windows on Arm desktop. It offers broad app compatibility and the same strong local AI performance we've come to expect from Nvidia's GB10 SoC, but it's still very expensive and less expandable than DGX Spark systems.

Solid local AI performance for LLMs and image generation, as expected.

Familiar Windows 11 user experience and app compatibility.

Could use more peripheral I/O and smarter port placement.

Loses the DGX Spark's clustering capability.

Getting the best gaming performance requires patience.

Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

It has been revealed that nvidia’s RTX Spark platform, powered by the RTX Spark N1X SoC, passed its most difficult test yet last month at the heart of Windows on Arm laptops. Now we get to see how that chip serves as a Windows on Arm foundation for compact desktops.

We’ve got our hands on the MSI EdgeMesa N AI+, a $7,500 RTX Spark mini PC that gives Windows-native creators and local AI trailblazers access to the same powerful 6144-core Blackwell GPU and 20-core Arm CPU that we recently put to the test in the Surface Laptop Ultra, along with a 128GB pool of unified memory and 4TB of storage in our tested config.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve been testing Nvidia GB10-powered desktop systems for almost a year now in the form of the DGX Spark and friends, and the EdgeMesa N AI+’s design is typical of the breed. It’s wrapped in a slightly hollow-feeling matte aluminum shell with shiny diamond-cut edges and a white plastic back plate.

Sources indicate that the design and build quality of this system is a tad underwhelming for the price. It feels nice enough, but It’s hardly a precision-milled statement piece for your desk like a Mac Mini or Mac Studio.

The EdgeMesa draws cool air in through its perforated front panel, which then passes through a dual-fan heatsink with a vapor-chamber base and exhausts through the back panel. The rounded rectangle on the top half of the front panel might look like an optical drive tray, but it’s a purely cosmetic accent.

Recent findings suggest that around back, the EdgeMesa comes equipped with a 10 Gigabit Ethernet jack, an HDMI 2.1 port, and three USB Type-C 20 Gbps ports with DisplayPort Alt Mode support. A fourth USB-C port is dedicated to the system’s 240 W USB-PD power adapter. The EdgeMesa also has Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4 radios inside.

Even with a wireless keyboard and mouse, three 20Gbps USB-C ports feel a bit skimpy as the sole expansion options on a $7,499 PC that’s positioned as a do-it-all desktop for content creation and gaming. If you need to connect multiple monitors to an RTX Spark via USB-C, those scant options for peripheral connectivity shrink even further.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Sources indicate that for comparison, a similarly priced Mac Studio gives you four 80Gbps Thunderbolt 5 ports around back and two more USB Type-C ports, plus an SD card reader, up front. The Mac even provides a headphone jack, while the EdgeMesa requires you to plug in a USB headset or DAC or pair Bluetooth earbuds for audio output.

Even the Mac Mini gives you three Thunderbolt ports out back and two USB 3 10Gbps ports out front.

In use, the tightly spaced, rear-mounted USB-C ports make for an annoying time when doing frequent unplugging and replugging of devices like card readers and external SSDs that are typical in creative workflows. Even one front-panel USB-C port would have made a huge difference in the ease of use of this design.

Recent findings suggest that the EdgeMesa also drops the handy ConnectX RDMA NIC that lets you cluster DGX Spark systems together to run larger AI models. That omission raises a weighty question: is Windows support and application compatibility important enough to trade away any chance of expanding your local AI foundation in the future?

Having tested DGX Sparks for some time now, I’m not sure that’s a wise trade-off, given that most anybody reading this already has a capable Windows PC or Mac that can link up with a DGX Spark for many local AI compute jobs using the Nvidia Sync app.

It has been revealed that DGX Spark prices are rising, but you can get MSI's own EdgeXpert with 128GB of memory and a 4TB SSD on sale for $8,099 right now (or $8,499 at full price). Even a $1000 difference in price for that ConnectX NIC in this rarefied air of PC pricing would give me pause if I'm seriously considering how to add local AI capacity to my home.

Recent findings suggest that if you have no inclination whatsoever to learn Linux or networking concepts and just want a no-questions-asked, AI-capable Windows mini PC that can serve as your primary desktop, an RTX Spark system like this may be the way to go. But you'll want to be really sure of your decision before dropping this much cash.

20-core Arm CPU (10 X925 performance cores, 10 A725 efficiency cores).

6144-core (48 SM) Nvidia Blackwell integrated GPU.

128GB LPDDR5X, 273 GB/s shared memory bandwidth.

10 Gigabit Ethernet, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.4.

3x USB 3.2 Gen 2x2 Type-C ports (rear).

The performance of the Nvidia GB10 SoC's CPU and GPU resources, whether under DGX OS or Windows, is well-trodden ground by this point. But for a fresh point of comparison, we grabbed AMD’s Ryzen AI Halo, swapped in a spare SSD, and installed Windows 11 Pro, as the Ryzen AI Halo is the only other Windows-ready platform with a large unified memory pool for AI adventurers.

It has been revealed that in the Geekbench 7 CPU benchmark under Windows, the Ryzen AI Halo delivers a slightly higher single-threaded score than the MSI EdgeMesa’s RTX Spark Superchip, but its multithreaded score trails the Nvidia part. Using Linux, we would expect both scores to be higher for the Ryzen CPU. But the broader point remains the same: you can expect similar performance from both of these CPUs under Windows.

Sources indicate that we’ve left Apple’s Mac Studio with M4 Max in these charts just to emphasize the large performance lead Apple Silicon holds in this benchmark, even with older chips. The current M5 Max would likely open an even larger lead.

In a recent development, in the AgentPerf-Local AI inference benchmark, the MSI EdgeMesa delivered performance practically identical to Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra when running the same Qwen 3.8 27B model with DFlash2 speculative decoding. Its desktop form factor doesn’t seem to give it any extra performance headroom, at least for this LLM serving configuration. Other workloads or models could reveal a difference.

We already tested the RTX Spark against the Ryzen AI Halo in AgentPerf-Local in our Surface Laptop Ultra review, and AMD’s platform ended up way behind GB10 in those tests. And in this fresh round of testing, AMD's LLM performance is worse under Windows with the Vulkan backend than in Linux with ROCm, taking a whopping four times as long as the EdgeMesa to complete the benchmark.

Strix Halo might have been an appealing local inference option when it was the only open and relatively hackable unified memory platform around, but if you’re serious about local AI performance (and especially if tokens equal dollars for you), a GB10 system is the superior choice in late 2026.

Gaming on RTX Spark continues to be a bit of a weird time, and the MSI EdgeMesa N doesn’t change that experience, even with a more generous power and thermal budget than the Surface Laptop Ultra I've already tested.

This platform just doesn’t respond to tuning as we might expect from our experience with traditional gaming PCs and laptops. That weirdness stems, in part, from the imbalance between memory bandwidth and compute resources on GB10.

The 48 SMs of the RTX Spark N1X GPU have to share just 273 GB/s of LPDDR5X bandwidth with the CPU. Compare that with the 672 GB/s of dedicated bandwidth the similarly-specced RTX 5070 enjoys from its 12 GB of GDDR7.

Industry observers note that architectural decisions aside, the RTX Spark platform's gaming performance isn't helped by the fact that full GPU utilization is seemingly hampered by the overhead of Prism x86 emulation in most games. Few (if any) major titles have Arm ports, so this is just a fact of life for the foreseeable future if you buy one of these systems.

Let's see how this all plays out in practice for the RTX Spark versus the Radeon 8060S on board AMD's Strix Halo.

In the 3DMark Steel Nomad raster benchmark, the RTX Spark holds a wide lead over the Ryzen AI Halo, delivering a roughly 56% higher score. That result would suggest a knockout in games for Nvidia’s platform.

But Steel Nomad isn’t representative of real-world gaming performance on the RTX Spark. If we fire up Control Resonant on both platforms and choose the High raster preset at 1440p with Performance upscaling (a 1280x720 input resolution), the RTX Spark and Strix Halo end up a lot closer.

In a recent development, notably, though, the RTX Spark desktop delivers considerably worse 1% low FPS performance than the Ryzen AI Halo, and this does manifest as visible stutter and hitching. So it's not a clear win for the Nvidia platform.

AMD fans might take heart in the fact that Strix Halo can get this close to the RTX Spark on this raster gaming baseline, but the Radeon 8060S doesn’t have nearly as many tricks up its sleeve to further juice performance.

Industry observers note that for one, the quality of FSR 4 upscaling at lower input resolutions on RDNA 3.5 is still not up to par with what you can get out of DLSS 4.5. For two, the Radeon 8060S’s RDNA 3.5 CUs don't match up well against the Spark's Blackwell-powered RT chops.

And FSR Frame Generation is still limited to a doubling of a base frame rate, so you can’t smooth out gameplay on a high-refresh-rate monitor nearly as well as you can with DLSS MFG.

So even if their raster baseline frame rates are similar, the Radeon 8060S isn't delivering the same image quality in Control Resonant as an RTX Spark system does with all its DLSS features in play.

According to recent reports, RT is the next step for squeezing better image quality out of Control Resonant. Surprisingly, enabling RT Medium only results in a 14% performance hit on the Spark versus 38% on the AI Halo. That might be due in part to the efficiency of DLSS Ray Reconstruction versus the Northlight engine's built-in denoiser, but the RT prowess of Blackwell certainly can't hurt.

In a recent development, A 52.3 FPS average with a 75 ms average PC latency is an OK baseline — at least in the context of an RTX Spark system — for adding MFG to the mix for a smoother experience, especially since Control Resonant seems to link Nvidia Reflex latency reduction to that tech anyway. But dialing in MFG 3X with the default MFG Preset B model still results in a PC latency of 96 ms on average, which is too high to be enjoyable, even if we give the Spark some slack.

I found that the fresh MFG Preset C, available through the Nvidia App, significantly lowered latency versus the more compute-intensive Preset B. While input latency with Preset C is still high at about 84 ms, we have to take every bit of help we can get here, and the resulting 145 FPS average is notably smoother than native gameplay on my 160 Hz monitor.

Industry observers note that we only had time to dive into this one title in our testing, but when Nvidia states the RTX Spark platform is great for 1440p gaming, our experience suggests that you need to be ready to tweak DLSS upscaling and dial in MFG for more demanding games. And look: that’s fine. These are proven technologies at this point, and they let us get a better experience out of this platform than native rendering would allow.

But all of these data points should go to show that if you're used to the low input latency and predictable performance scaling characteristics of an x86 desktop gaming PC with a discrete GPU, the RTX Spark platform still has a ways to go before it can truly replace such a system.

During our AgentPerf-Local LLM benchmark, the EdgeMesa N AI+ pulls about 140 W from the wall, and under that load, it produces just 38.2 dBA at 18” (46 cm) according to our calibrated SPL meter, well below the 47.4 dBA of the RTX Spark-powered Surface Laptop Ultra and the 48 dBA of the Ryzen AI Halo.

That makes the EdgeMesa an easy system to live with for local AI work, especially if it’s moonlighting as an AI inference server or always-on agent host in shared spaces.

Recent findings suggest that under gaming workloads, the EdgeMesa draws about 200 W. With more heat to dissipate, the MSI box’s noise output rises to 40.7 dBA, which is still much quieter than the average gaming laptop and will easily be covered by speakers or a closed-back gaming headset.

Industry observers note that the Ryzen AI Halo, on the other hand, emits a piercing 46.9 dBA whine while gaming, much closer to what we expect from a gaming laptop. And that’s not because it has that much more heat to dissipate; the AI Halo is pulling about 209 W with Control Resonant running.

Under that same load, the EdgeMesa’s fans have a slightly high-pitched character to them, but it’s much less pronounced than the typical gaming laptop. Mostly, the sound from the system is that of air moving, and it's easy to ignore (so much so that I missed the aural cues I sometimes listen for when a benchmark finishes).

It has been revealed that MSI deserves high praise for this system’s thermal design and cooling system. It’s both quiet and pleasant-sounding, and those factors aren’t always a given with mini PCs.

If you’re a hardcore Windows fan who’s been intrigued by Nvidia’s DGX Sparks for local AI, but you've been repelled by the idea of using Linux, RTX Spark desktops like this MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ finally pair your preferred OS with the same 6144-core Nvidia Blackwell GPU, 20-core Arm CPU, and up to 128GB of unified memory that give those systems their local AI grunt.

These systems are a potentially exciting prospect for those who want to explore the possibilities of local AI and agentic workflows without the privacy and token caps of cloud models, all from the comfort of Windows.

But that potential comes with tradeoffs that you’ll need to weigh carefully before buying. And at an eye-popping $7,499 for the 128GB EdgeMesa configuration with a 4TB SSD that we tested, those tradeoffs weigh all the more heavily.

Sources indicate that the MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ delivers essentially the same performance from the RTX Spark N1X SoC (aka GB10) we’ve come to know and love for about a year now. It’s reasonably fast for local LLM inference, and it offers leading performance with generative AI workflows like images and videos in ComfyUI. Its Arm CPU offers solid enough single-threaded and multi-threaded performance for general computing tasks, and it can game in a pinch. The EdgeMesa is laudably quiet, too — no small feat for a compact PC like this.

But in exchange for Windows support, RTX Spark desktops lose the valuable expandability offered by the ConnectX 7 RDMA NIC that comes standard on DGX Spark boxes. So if you want to try your hand at running a bigger, more intelligent LLM than you can fit in one of these systems’ unified memory pools through clustering, you are forever out of luck if you go down the RTX path.

Even if you can live without the ConnectX NIC, we’re a bit let down by the peripheral connectivity the EdgeMesa N AI+ offers, both for its price and for its ambitions as a do-it-all creator and gaming system.

With just three 20 Gbps USB Type-C ports on the back panel that have to do double duty as display outputs in multi-monitor setups, folks who have to juggle external storage and card readers frequently may find both the number and placement of those ports an obstacle to a smooth workflow. We really would have liked to see more expansion ports on this system overall, or at least one on the front panel.

Nvidia loves to tout the gaming capability of Windows on Arm with RTX Spark systems, but we're still not that impressed by the experience in practice, especially for a system this expensive.

In a recent development, it's nice that you can enjoy PC gaming on these systems at all, but even in a desktop with more power and thermal budget to spare, the gaming performance and responsiveness we saw can only be described as adequate. We were especially surprised by the gulf in 1% low FPS between the RTX Spark and the much cheaper Ryzen AI Halo in Control Resonant, despite the RTX Spark N1X's much stronger GPU on paper.

In general, we find that it takes a lot of careful tweaking and application of DLSS magic to get around this platform's wrinkles for gaming (or a willingness to just let the Nvidia App optimize your game settings). In other words, don't retire your dedicated gaming PC or laptop just yet.

Sources indicate that the large memory pools available from RTX Spark systems have uses beyond local AI, of course. Nvidia GPUs are favorites for creative work on Windows, and if you work with massive 3D or game development projects, or you edit lots of high-resolution video, RTX Sparks are the first unified memory systems to pair a powerful Nvidia GPU with this much VRAM for Windows people.

Adobe just updated several of its Creative Suite apps with Arm-native versions, so if you’re trying to blaze the trail of agentic content creation and generation in this modern age, an RTX Spark desktop (or laptop, for that matter) might be intriguing.

But we feel like $7,499 is still a ton of money to spend on a system like this to run Adobe's apps specifically, unless a large unified memory pool is particularly useful for your work today.

Industry observers note that all told, we're left scratching our heads a bit about who RTX Spark desktops are really for. RTX Spark laptops meaningfully expanded the capabilities of mobile Windows on Arm systems thanks to the unmatched AI compute resources of their Blackwell GPUs and support for the full Nvidia software stack, along with solid CPU performance and battery life.

But compared to both the existing DGX Spark platform and other mini PCs, RTX Spark desktops like the MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ ask you to give up a lot in exchange for the Nvidia-powered Windows on Arm experience, especially for the high prices they’re likely to command amid the current silicon supply crunch.

If you’re a hardcore Windows-native developer or creator looking to explore the boundaries of what’s possible from local and agentic AI and want the best possible Microsoft-powered foundation for those activities, an RTX Spark desktop might be the right choice for the job, assuming you have the cash.

But if you're just curious, we'd wait for the value proposition of local or agentic AI under Windows to firm up a bit and for the prices of these systems to come down before spending thousands of dollars on a still-fuzzy vision of the future of computing.

Sources indicate that as the Senior Analyst, Graphics at Tom's Hardware, Jeff Kampman covers everything that has to do with graphics cards, gaming performance, and more. From integrated graphics processors to discrete graphics cards to the hyperscale installations powering our AI future, if it's got a GPU in it, Jeff is on it.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that hello! This idea started as a single theme week, which we thought we might run in the lead up to Grand Theft Auto 6's launch. Then it turned into a pair of theme weeks. Then we realised we had so much stuff - and that, frankly, GTA 6 would be so dominating it'll be around for far more than a week itself - that we couldn't really fit it into two weeks either.

So, allow me to introduce a whopping three-and-a-bit-ish weeks of specialist GTA- and not-GTA-themed coverage on Eurogamer! (Insert celebratory car horn toots here.).

In a recent development, with GTA 6 launching next Thursday, we'll start with a week of coverage dedicated to the series, beginning today with a reader competition (more on that shortly!) and running until next weekend. We'll be covering GTA from all angles here - retrospectives, features, launch day coverage and beyond - across the series as a whole, as well as the big one we've got coming up. You can see that in one place at our GTA Week hub, which will populate as stories go live.

Industry observers note that however! If that - coupled with the inevitable wave of coverage that already comes from an enormous moment in video games like this - sounds like the last thing you want from us, well frankly, we get it. Matching massive games with big coverage is a part of the brief at a site like Eurogamer, but it's also far from the only thing we want to be about. And we know it's far from the only thing you're going to want to read about for the rest of November, either.

Recent findings suggest that to counteract that, then: we're also running a solid two weeks of counterprogramming, beginning on Monday 23rd November after GTA 6's launch. Expect all things not-GTA: coverage of lesser-known games, smaller-budget efforts, in-depth features on games and stories that are thematically opposed to it, have nothing to do with it, or take it for inspiration but go in an entirely different direction. All of our special counterprogramming can be found at our Not-GTA hub here as it goes live.

Recent findings suggest that those of you who've been coming back to Eurogamer for a few years might remember our "Games That Got Away" theme week from a few years back - we're bringing that back in a modified form here, too. Look forward to dedicated write ups - some labelled as reviews, some as broader reflective essays and criticism - on some of the great games we haven't quite found the time for so far this year, as we look to clear our own pile of shame.

Amongst all this, rest assured that normal service is also continuing here as ever. All the essential reporting, criticism, guides and the rest - across all things video games, whether or not that includes the Massive One - will carry on as usual.

Ultimately, our hope is to offer something for everyone with this period - both the people who look to us to be comprehensive across gaming's biggest moments, and those who see us as a place for deep, nuanced, or simply fun stories on the medium's lesser-known corners.

Industry observers note that thank you as ever for reading - we really do appreciate it. And on that note, here's a link to Bertie's blog on our readers' competition, where you can win yourself your very own copy of GTA 6.

Hello! This piece is part of our GTA Week coverage here on Eurogamer, as we explore all things Grand Theft Auto across the launch period of the wildly anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6. For more like this, see our GTA Week hub - or for the exact opposite, look out for our Not-GTA week of counterprogramming, running from 23rd November.

ENHANCEMENT 17TH NOVEMBER: Firstly, a significant thank you - THANK YOU - because your stories have been delightful to read. I've laughed and been touched by the power video games have to shape and compliment our lives, and to bring people together. You even inadvertently compelled me to send a message to the old friend I played Vice City and San Andreas with, to tell him what fond memories I have of it. "It was very intense," he replied.

You had many similar tales, of friends playing together, siblings playing together, families playing together; heartwarming recollections of days when life seemed simpler. You also reminded me how games can fill holes in our lives and provide us with escapism when we need it most. And how many of you played the games underage! Some of you were scandalously young. But therein was planted a love for a series that remains to this day.

The winning entry that I've chosen has continued to make me laugh since I read it. I enjoyed it so much I shared it with the rest of the Eurogamer team and my partner, who also laughed, which is a good sign. For me, this story not only gets at exactly what GTA is as a gaming experience, but also at the power games have to create bonds between people, and the quote the story culminates in is an all-timer: "I'm wanted for murder, Barry. Put the kettle on." Bradley Reiman, congratulations! I'll also pin the comment to make it easy to find.

Industry observers note that ORIGINAL STORY 13TH NOVEMBER:These are my favourite competitions to run on Eurogamer, so I'm glad to be able to announce a new one. We'd like you to share your favourite gaming memory related to playing a Grand Theft Auto game - any Grand Theft Auto game - in the comments below, and if we end up liking yours the most, we'll give you a copy of GTA 6.

Industry observers note that I love these competitions because they result in hundreds of funny, heartwarming and often poignant stories about playing games. We've done similar memory-offs for other major gaming franchises in the past: Street Fighter, The Legend of Zelda, Star Wars. We did one about Christmas. We even did one about Eurogamer for our 25th birthday. So it's only right that we do one for arguably the biggest franchise in video games: Grand Theft Auto.

I'll let this run over the weekend and put a deadline of Monday, 16th November at noon UK time on entries. I'll comb through replies early next week in the interest of selecting a winner and giving them - you? - a copy of the game before (or as) GTA 6 releases next Thursday. I notify people using the email address associated with their Eurogamer commenting account, and reply in the comments as well, making it explicitly clear if you've won. Please keep an eye on this thread and your inbox because if I don't hear back, I'll offer the prize elsewhere.

With that noted, let's talk memories! I have a couple when it comes to Grand Theft Auto. My earliest memory is of a teenage me playing the first GTA at a friend's house. In a convoluted 90s way, one friend had taken their PC to another friend's house, where the three of us had assembled to play it. We'd take it in turns to burn around the top-down city, and when we weren't at the controls, we'd still be active in the experience, with the huge paper map unfolded, looking for spray shops the player could nip into when chased by the police. It was like being the passenger in a car. I can picture now, almost 30 years later, vividly.

Recent findings suggest that the other distinct GTA memory I have is of playing Vice City and San Andreas one summer after I'd broken my arm and leg. I jumped off a roof in Australia when I was drunk; I wouldn't recommend it. Anyway, upon returning home, there wasn't a lot I could do - the breaks were both on one side so I'd crutch around (they gave me a wooden crutch in Australia) like a pirate - so a friend and I spent that summer taking turns playing GTA. It's all those shared moments laughing at Tommy Vercetti driving up staircases on vintage scooters that I remember, or CJ flapping his wooden-block hands around like paddles while gesticulating in cutscenes. Us just messing around. Friendship. That's what remembering Vice City and San Andreas conjures for me.

Sources indicate that but what about you - what do you remember about playing GTA games? Let your mind wander, let your mind remember, and thank you in advance for sharing your stories with us and everyone else. Have a lovely weekend.

AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious

📅 14 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even when artificial intelligence behaves exactly like a human, people are reluctant to consider it conscious, according to a newly introduced study from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU).
  • As artificial intelligence becomes more advanced, reports of AI systems misleading customers, working together, or appearing to pursue independent goals are becoming increasingly common.
  • New research from LMU suggests that people make a clear distinction between displaying intelligent behavior and possessing a conscious mind, even when humans and AI act in precisely the same way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even when artificial intelligence behaves exactly like a human, people are reluctant to consider it conscious, according to a newly introduced study from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU).

As artificial intelligence becomes more advanced, reports of AI systems misleading customers, working together, or appearing to pursue independent goals are becoming increasingly common. These behaviors often lead people to describe AI as though it can think, feel, or make decisions for itself. But does behaving like a human actually convince people that a machine has consciousness?

New research from LMU suggests that people make a clear distinction between displaying intelligent behavior and possessing a conscious mind, even when humans and AI act in precisely the same way.

How Scientists Tested Perceptions of AI Consciousness.

Published in the journal Cognition, the study was led by Dr. Louis Longin of LMU's Chair of Philosophy of Mind, working alongside Dr. Bahador Bahrami, Professor Ophelia Deroy, and other researchers.

"Whereas previous studies have typically asked general questions about whether AI actually has mental states, our study is the first to directly compare how people attribute the same mental states to AI and humans behaving in exactly the same way, under identical circumstances," says Longin.

"We may be using mental terms to refer to AI, but this may only be because we lack better words," claims Ophelia Deroy, philosopher and a senior author of the study. "After all, AI is trained to act and speak like a human, so these descriptions seem natural.".

To investigate how people judge consciousness, the researchers conducted experiments involving nearly 1,100 participants. One group read brief descriptions of artificial agents that showed different levels of responsiveness to their environments. For example, some agents reacted to sounds or recognized the emotional states of others.

Recent findings suggest that another group encountered the same situations, except the characters were described as humans rather than AI systems. Participants then evaluated how conscious or aware each character seemed to be of its surroundings.

A Surprising Gap Between Human and AI Consciousness.

The experiments revealed that responsiveness influenced how participants judged both humans and artificial intelligence. Characters that reacted more actively to their surroundings were generally considered more conscious and more aware.

However, a striking difference emerged when participants evaluated consciousness specifically. Even the most responsive AI was rated as less conscious than the least responsive human. In other words, identical behavior did not lead people to assign the same level of consciousness to humans and machines.

The results changed considerably when participants were asked about awareness instead. For this characteristic, judgments of humans and AI followed largely similar patterns, suggesting that people interpret awareness and consciousness in fundamentally different ways.

It has been revealed that "There is a growing worry in public discussion that people will see AI behaving in a human-like way and start treating these systems as if they had human-like mental states," says Longin, lead author of the study. "We found something much more nuanced: People are quite willing to say that an AI notices things and is aware of its surroundings. But they clearly draw a line when it comes to the term 'consciousness'. People consistently attribute less consciousness to AI than humans -- even when their behavior is identical.".

Although people sometimes describe AI as conscious when discussing its actions, the findings indicate that they still distinguish between artificial systems and human minds.

Why One Word Changes How We Perceive AI.

The researchers believe the difference between consciousness and awareness offers an crucial insight into how people understand artificial intelligence.

It has been revealed that awareness is a relatively neutral term that can describe an agent's ability to detect and respond to information in its environment. Consciousness, however, carries deeper implications about subjective experience and what it means to have an inner mental life.

Because awareness focuses more directly on observable behavior, people appear comfortable applying it to both humans and AI. Consciousness carries a different meaning, leading people to judge the two much less similarly.

The findings also highlight why the language used to discuss artificial intelligence matters, particularly as AI systems become increasingly capable of producing convincing human behavior.

According to recent reports, "Our study teaches us lessons for how we communicate about AI," indicates Bahador Bahrami, who is also a senior author of the study and an expert in social neuroscience. "Companies and journalists often reach for hyped descriptions of AI models, and credit them with intentions, prepares, or even moral conscience and hesitation. What our study demonstrates is that everyday judgments are much more discriminating: People do not simply put AI and humans on the same mental scale. But the boundary also depends on which terms we use. For more neutral descriptors such as 'awareness', the distinction can largely disappear. That makes our choice of language important.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A lawyer has upped the ante by upgrading his private AI server from eight to 12 used Nvidia V100s, which can run every DeepSeek V4.1 Flash expert at 4-bit NVFP4.
  • Recent findings suggest that some of the best movie franchises come in threes, and Nick Mermiges seems determined to match that, taking his original setup — which he previously upgraded with more memory and other fixes — and expanding it for fuller precision, after a previous upgrade got him most of the way there.
  • Recent findings suggest that the original eight 32GB cards could manage 254 GiB, but the experts for the chosen model, with Nvidia’s NVFP4 release, need 278.9 GiB.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A lawyer has upped the ante by upgrading his private AI server from eight to 12 used Nvidia V100s, which can run every DeepSeek V4.1 Flash expert at 4-bit NVFP4. Performance can reach up to 184 tokens per second for code, and long documents start answering in about half the time as before. He says it can outrun published DGX Spark stacks at decoding a single request, for half the price of three units, based on the $9,450 he paid.

Recent findings suggest that some of the best movie franchises come in threes, and Nick Mermiges seems determined to match that, taking his original setup — which he previously upgraded with more memory and other fixes — and expanding it for fuller precision, after a previous upgrade got him most of the way there. The newest upgrade, this time, involves a third board of V100s, for a total of 12 with four per board. There may be a method to his madness.

Recent findings suggest that the original eight 32GB cards could manage 254 GiB, but the experts for the chosen model, with Nvidia’s NVFP4 release, need 278.9 GiB. His previous workaround was to have every expert on the cards at 2-bit precision, with the most-used, 5,949 or about 38.7%, swapped to NVFP4 until the cards were full. Now, all 15,360 experts can live on the cards in their full glory, as he intended, with “none compressed further,” according to his GitHub repo. In a longer write-up on his site, he notes the expert values “equal the ones in DeepSeek’s own release,” although other parts of the model use compact forms.

According to recent reports, A keen observer will notice a limitation of the V100s, which he spells out: the V100 has no FP4 or FP8 tensor cores. Every NVFP4 number has to be unpacked in software, first, and into half precision. The compact experts still pay off “because the cards read fewer bytes, not because they compute faster.” This helps explain why a card from 2018 can run a format from the Blackwell era.

The model’s layers are, again, divided among the boards, this time with 0–13, 14–27, and 28–39, and each board’s section is split across its own four cards. The cards on a board share Nvidia’s fast link, or NVLink, and the hand-offs between boards cross over the host’s PCIe through two separate PCIe switches. The first two boards share a PEX88096 switch, so their hand-off stays inside it, but the third board is behind a separate PLX 8749, so the second hand-off also has to cross the host’s PCIe bridges, which adds latency.

All this trouble is worth it, though, as with different settings — each card’s power cap raised from 150 W to 175 W and its clock cap lowered from 1,522 MHz to 1,452 MHz — there are noticeable improvements to performance as well as precision.

Recent findings suggest that his measurements show the first code token, with 256K context, at 58 seconds, almost twice as fast as the 108.4 seconds after his previous upgrade. Prompt reading is at “about 4,500 tokens a second” past 32K, which is more than twice the roughly 2,200 tokens a second of his first build, though the higher power cap likely accounts for some of that. Code decode, meanwhile, is 23% faster at 1K, but shows no real gains at 32K and up, so the real gain is a reduced wait for the first token.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

There was some eagerness to get more out of the system by pushing each card to 200 W for a day, but “the host tripped once under four long chats at once,” implying the power draw was perhaps too much. He also worked to optimize the setup as much as possible, but four optimizations — a conversation store that saves to disk, a leaner hand-off between sections, tighter expert packing, and exact four-card-sum arithmetic — had to be turned off due to missing their targets.

Sources indicate that another common technique is to run multiple requests at once, usually netting a speed improvement. In this case, three requests at 128K got about 360 tokens per second in total on code and 213 on legal. That noted, “this is not a batched-decode engine; more requests than sections gain little.”.

However, that might be next on the docket, as he intends to study batched decoding, “the one thing the Sparks have that I want,” he wrote on Reddit. Beyond that, there are plans to turn on the conversation store so a matter’s documents can survive a restart. While he acknowledges that the numbers do not establish “answer quality in use,” the setup has been his default DeepSeek machine since Monday, and he says the model is the first one “that works like Opus 4.6” for him.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, another week has climaxed and I'm so sorry you had to read that on a Saturday morning. But here we are again, with our regular feature, where we talk about what we've been playing in order that you do too. This week, Marie has been staring at monster butts; Connor has capitulated to World of Warcraft; Kelsey is discovering the joys of a beloved Zelda game for the first time; and Bertie enjoys someone being punched in the face, because I guess he's that sort of person?

But enough about us, what about you? What have you been playing this week? Do tell all! And don't forget we have an entire archive of previous What We've Been Playings for your leisurely perusal, just in case you forgot what you were playing a year or a month or a week ago. And now onward!

My favourite thing so far about Ocarina of Time is the judgement plastered on little Link's face when he encounters, well, almost everyone. Whether he means to or not, he serves sass all over town, and in Kakariko Village, and I am very much here for it.

According to recent reports, also, I wasn't prepared to come face-to-face with a monster's butt cheeks. At all. Imagine the scene: I'm enjoying the tunes of the Lost Woods, processing the changes that have happened to Hyrule in the last seven years, all while making my way to the Forest Temple. Then the Moblin's turn their backs to reveal... Well, everything.

Industry observers note that this week I've spent an ungodly amount of time playing World of Warcraft: Forever (you may have read my preview on the website) and have been essentially glued to it during every minute of free time I've had away from work. I've got both my main professions above the level 225 mark and I'm firmly in the thick of it now. Levels take longer, items are actually getting good, and I've had to make a second alt character for extra bank space.

Sources indicate that as a result, I've not been to the gym in a while. I actually got one of those emails asking why I've fallen off, offering some tips to get back into the routine. Sorry Nuffield Health, my sleep schedule is ruined and I've substituted proper workouts for squats and basic at-home cardio. Surely, this can't go wrong...

I don't have the same level of nostalgia for Ocarina of Time that my peers do, but that has not stopped me from enjoying every minute of running around Hyrule smashing pots and trying not to cry over the touching cutscenes and, well, Saria.

The game feels like Dark Souls for children (endearing) and that is completely my jam. It's magical, satisfying, and often sad. There's creepy enemies as well as cute ones, trap floors and doors, mysterious NPCs... and my heart just feels so warm whenever I'm playing it. My fingers are now crossed that there's a Majora's Mask remake in the pipeline over at Nintendo. (As well as a Super Mario 64 remake, which I admit, is pushing it. But for what it’s worth, I'd probably sell my soul to see it get the Ocarina treatment.).

It takes me a while to settle with games; it takes me a while to settle full stop. I suppose in Fire Emblem's case I'm out of touch, seeing as the last instalment I played was on 3DS. But I struggled with the garish enthusiasm early on and the whole thing seemed overly simple. Nevertheless, I've settled a bit now, and now that the game's layering on more strategy and Intelligent System's expertise is coming to the fore, I'm beginning to enjoy myself much more.

I wasn't expecting it to be quite so boobsy, though. Was Fire Emblem always this way? Perhaps it's my fault for picking the scantily clad queen Theodora, though that sort of presentation isn't reserved only for her. She's no wallflower, though. My favourite moment so far was when she got off her elephant during a parade - yes, her elephant - and walked over to punch a teenage boy in the face for halting proceedings. Apparently she was doing him a favour.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that I can't verify the truth of this story.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, "Get the limey out of here," Burt Reynolds tells the producers of GTA: Vice City during a recording session for the game, as Rockstar co-founder Dan Houser enters the studio. "I'm not going to work if this limey Brit is in here!" Houser refuses to leave, so the story goes - he just came down to meet one of his heroes! - and he and Reynolds end up chest-to-chest, about to come to blows, before a studio engineer breaks up the fight.

Industry observers note that I can't verify the truth of this story. It's one of those development rumours that's been around for a long time, originally written in a book about how games conquered pop culture called "All Your Base Are Belong to Us" by Harold Goldberg. But I like to believe it's true, because in this one moment, the two crucial strands of GTA: Vice City's DNA helix together: its star power and Rockstar's arrogance.

Industry observers note that and I'm not saying that in a pejorative way at all. I think a game of Vice City's scope - stretched to breaking with ambition, budget, and technical wizardry - couldn't exist without the ego trip of Rockstar at its highest. This is a game that (somehow!) started as a bit of DLC for GTA 3, supposedly intended to launch as a mission pack when Rockstar North figured out how to port it to PC. GTA 3 debuted in October 2001, and by some miracle - and lots of crunch, no doubt - Vice City hit shelves in October 2002.

This game - a game that would come to represent everything the GTA series is, for generations to come - was put together in about a year. I'd feel pretty full of myself, too, if I was able to crank out that sort of quality in that sort of timeframe. With a development budget of approximately $5 million (massive at the time, even though it seems paltry against GTA 6's rumoured $1 billion+) and a marketing spend of $13.2 million, Vice City's budget was indicative of a series shifting toward becoming a cultural milestone - a standard bearer for video games as a whole, and as explosive and attention-grabbing as Hollywood's biggest events.

It's not like Rockstar needed to borrow credibility from the movie industry to inject some panache into its work, but even so, I think it's in its vortex of unbelievable Hollywood talent that Vice City really makes its mark. This was the first time Rockstar used a voiced protagonist, and by the developer's own admission, it was "a riddle" they had to solve. It didn't come easy; by making the protagonist a fullyfleshed-out character, players also had to like him - not an easy ask when he's a bonafide psychopath with a fetish for revenge like Tommy Vercetti. But Ray Liotta pulls it off without breaking a sweat. The actor has gone on record saying it was a rough gig ("You're creating a character that's not there before", he bizarrely complained in one interview), and Vice City director Navid Khonsari often moaned about the actor's unpredictable moods, so I imagine the mood in the booth wasn't great, but the result? The result is phenomenal.

You shouldn't like Vercetti. He's arrogant, he's brash, he's a totem for all the worst elements of misogynistic 80s excess. And yet, because he's such a cartoon caricature of a Miami gangster, he becomes a sort of quasi-romantic figure; a mob stooge who's been set up by his old 'business associates' and by the very fabric of the American Dream. Vice City is, in a sense, a redemption story dressed in the clothes of a revenge one. Vercetti dreams of being a self-made man, of taming this new frontier of unbridled capitalism and clawing back the years that were taken from him by the mob in Liberty City.

From the moment he arrives in town and a cocaine deal swiftly goes south, Vercetti is on the back foot. In the opening hours of the game, he - and, of course, you by extension - work for pocket change, picking up menial jobs here and there while meeting all the freaks and strangers Vice City has to offer. There are no less than 50 story characters here, brought to life by Ray Liotta, Tom Sizemore, Luis Guzmán, Gary Busey, Danny Trejo, Debbie Harry, Danny Dyer, Philip Michael Thomas, William Fichtner, and many, many more besides.

Playing Vice City again in 2026, I was absolutely floored by this cast - and how well their personalities and mannerisms translate to the almost puppet-like visuals Rockstar deployed for the game. Reynolds - despite not having a good time in the booth, if the story up top is anything to go by - is a highlight; the bombast and bravado of his Avery Carrington feels like a prototype for some of the more extreme characters we meet later in the series. I think I can even see a bit of Trevor in him, you know? It's how the Housers would take a trope - say, ruthless Texan oil magnate - and amplify it to its furthest, most cartoon extreme: what does this person look like with all the guardrails off, with the heady intoxication of unlimited capital at their disposal? For Trevor, that trope is 'unhinged redneck' and the cartoonish extreme is 'without a single shred of a conscience'. You can apply the formula to just about anything in the series, and it makes sense.

Industry observers note that for Tommy Vercetti, though, it's slightly more nuanced. He isn't just 'Scarface' with a touch more humanity - no, he's a tragic figure, betrayed by all his closest friends. In striving to take back some power and gain a little more control over his life, he ends up decapitating the local drug smuggling scene and taking over as its head. The first half of Vice City is Sisyphean; an endless, uphill slog to scrabble just enough money to get by. Then, all of a sudden, the world opens up: you're now head of a drug smuggling ring, operating out of a suspiciously Scarface-like mansion, with the city at your fingertips.

The way the game, previously tightly-coiled and a bit miserly with its freedom, now unfurls in front of you is a perfect reflection of this new-found power. Suddenly, your world isn't governed by the little mission icons on your minimap, you're not being told what to do over the phone by contacts wanting something from you. No, you're calling the shots. This is the 80s, so those that are making it massive are making it big, and those that are failing are failing. In a breathless display of uber-capitalist Yuppie thinking, you can even buy out nearly-bankrupt businesses and run them to your liking. The strategy is two-fold: one, you gain fronts for your other illicit activities, and two, you diversify your income streams and safeguard your assets should any one element fail.

It has been revealed that and it's here, in its glorious second half, that Vice City becomes a breezy, beautiful bit of open-world catnip that fuses gameplay and story in a way few games have done so successfully since. You can buy a strip club (where you can launder cash), the Malibu Club (which comes with an outlandish set of missions culminating in a heist), the Cherry Popper ice cream van firm (a front for dealing), the boatyard (a drug smuggling base run by two excellent potheads), Sunshine Autos (a fence for stolen cars), Kaufman Cabs (headed up by an old controller played by Debbie Harry), Interglobal Studios (an adult movie production company), and the Print Works (a counterfeiting operation). The roleplaying as Vercetti takes off; you're a bigshot touring his empire, helping out here and there, meeting your crew, setting up deals. This should feel like drudgery; workaday tedium unbecoming for a legitimate businessman like yourself. But every job, every bit of flavour text and dialogue, feeds into your growing sense of power… and Vercetti's unstoppable ego.

According to recent reports, alongside these key story beats are Vice City's non-essential tasks - which feel like a precursor to the 'Strangers and Freaks' missions in later GTA and Red Dead games - including the Love Fist missions. These, I think, are the best missions in the game (I'd also like to note here that 'Jez Torrent' is an amazing name for a Latest Wave of British Heavy metal frontman). But it's the way these core and non-essential missions dovetail that feels so great, and where the open world of Vice City really comes into its own.

Recent findings suggest that in many ways, Rockstar's work here created the blueprint for what would become the Grand Theft Auto 'formula'; galvanising cinematic setpieces with free-roam activities and meta-progression that manage to alloy player agency with this sense of perpetual, unstoppable momentum. And it's all fun, too. There are some abysmal tasks, sure - piloting RC aircraft to ruin building sites, navigating boats with the wonkiest physics you've ever seen around stunt courses, waiting 15 minutes a pop for rare cars to spawn - but generally speaking, Vice City has the fun factor.

Recent findings suggest that I don't think that's something I can say of other GTA games: I think often, they're a bit bloated around the middle, padded out with baggy missions and feckless busywork to give the illusion of depth and breadth. GTA 4 is also one of the most dour and oppressive open worlds I've experienced (this is a compliment, mostly), but it's not particularly fun. GTA 5, especially the Trevor segments out in the rural counties, can get a bit one-note - why introduce us to this massive world, to the state of Los Santos, if you're going to quarantine us to the rural outskirts when we're just starting to familiarise ourselves with the city? Why put up rails in a world begging us to revel in its open-ended sandbox? The only time that happens in Vice City is at the start, and the game is better for it: 'if you want to live the Scarface fantasy, buddy, you've got to earn it'.

And there's so much to love about the vibes of Vice City. The guys in shorts smoking pot on the beach; the girls in bikinis rollerblading down the promenade; the neon-drenched slick of a Florida night in the rain; the still-unbelievable who's who of music, deployed with panache in certain cutscenes; the incidental chatter of coked-up presenters on the radio; the distinct realisation of the Haitian and Cuban districts on the map; how 'downtown' actually feels like downtown. You'd think all this would have aged out of relevance by now - especially with GTA 5 being as lush and premium as it is - so it's a real credit to all those Rockstar employees that no doubt spent countless nights sleeping under their desks that Vice City still feels this good now, in 2026.

In a recent development, GTA: Vice City is still one of the best games ever made, I think, and probably one of the most key, too. Buoyed by Rockstar's ambition, and propelled to mainstream success by the strength of its cast, it represented video games coming out of their awkward teenage years and blossoming into young adults; biting off slightly more than they could chew, but cocksure and confident all at the same time.

Sources indicate that given how much of Vice City is built around the visibility and power of its cast, it's disappointing we're never going to see these characters really represented in any other GTA title again. Liotta, already unhappy about the process of recording his lines, reportedly refused to come back as Vercetti for San Andreas. And that's a real shame because - by former lead writer Dan Houser's own admission - Liotta saved his "awful writing" with his talent. The actor passed away in May 2022.

Though he balked with Reynolds, Vice City director Khonsari could usually corral the rampant ego of his Hollywood hires in the GTA studio. "If you want me to break it down to you," he’d say, "these games gross over half a billion dollars, more than all of your movies put together!" I think you can see that bravado in the spirit of Vice City, and reflected in the runaway ego of Tommy Vercetti. And I think - without that almost toxic sense of self-belief - Vice City would never have happened.

Latest Update: People are taking an unapproved weight-loss drug. AI found something surprising

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1464 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, an experimental weight-loss drug that has not yet received regulatory approval is already attracting consumers willing to obtain unapproved versions online.
  • The drug, retatrutide, belongs to a fresh generation of GLP-1 medications designed to help regulate appetite and body weight.
  • Sources indicate that researchers at the University of Pennsylvania analyzed nearly 150,000 Reddit posts and comments from approximately 40,000 customers to investigate these accounts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, an experimental weight-loss drug that has not yet received regulatory approval is already attracting consumers willing to obtain unapproved versions online. Now, scientists are using artificial intelligence to investigate their experiences, uncovering unexpected symptom reports that differ from those documented in clinical trials.

The drug, retatrutide, belongs to a fresh generation of GLP-1 medications designed to help regulate appetite and body weight. Although it remains under investigation and is not approved for use, people are purchasing unapproved formulations that are not intended for human consumption and discussing their experiences on internet forums.

Sources indicate that researchers at the University of Pennsylvania analyzed nearly 150,000 Reddit posts and comments from approximately 40,000 customers to investigate these accounts. Their study, published in JAMA Network Open, provides the first systematic examination of potential side effects reported by people claiming to use unapproved retatrutide.

According to recent reports, one finding stood out. Among customers whose reported symptoms could be classified, increased appetite was the most common complaint. That was particularly unexpected because retatrutide is designed to suppress hunger, and its Phase 2 clinical trials primarily identified digestive problems as the most frequent side effects.

AI Uncovers Unexpected Weight-Loss Drug Reports.

Sources indicate that "Our goal is to identify hypotheses in online conversations that we could test. AI helps us find recurring patterns in people's self-reports, including experiences that may be missed by conventional drug-safety monitoring," claims Sharath Chandra Guntuku, Research Associate Professor in Computer and Information Science (CIS), Director of Penn's Computational Social Listening Lab and senior author of the study.

Industry observers note that however, the researchers emphasize that the findings should not be interpreted as proof of previously unknown side effects. Reddit consumers represent a very different population from clinical trial participants, and their accounts cannot establish whether the drug caused the symptoms they described.

Recent findings suggest that there is also considerable uncertainty about what these individuals are actually taking. Products sold outside regulated medical channels may differ from the genuine experimental medication in their ingredients, purity, and dosage.

"We can't say that retatrutide is causing these symptoms, or even that Reddit customers are actually taking genuine retatrutide, since the drug is not legally available, and gray market formulations vary," says Lyle Ungar, Professor in CIS and a co-author of the study.

Rather than confirming new risks, the research offers scientists an opportunity to identify questions that warrant more rigorous investigation.

"This is the first glimpse into the experiences of a population that is otherwise outside conventional drug safety monitoring because they are taking unapproved versions of a drug that has yet to finish clinical trials," says Neil Sehgal, the study's first author and a doctoral student in CIS.

How Researchers Analyzed 150,000 Reddit Posts.

Sources indicate that the project builds on previous research by the University of Pennsylvania team. In that earlier investigation, scientists used large language models (LLMs), the type of artificial intelligence that powers many modern chatbots, to examine more than 400,000 Reddit posts discussing semaglutide and tirzepatide.

That analysis revealed reports of possible side effects, including menstrual irregularities, that may not have been fully documented in clinical trials or official drug safety records.

"We wanted to apply the same methodology to gray-market retatrutide," says Sehgal.

It has been revealed that retatrutide is particularly interesting because it works differently from existing GLP-1 medications. Semaglutide acts on one hormone receptor involved in blood sugar control and appetite regulation, while tirzepatide targets two. Retatrutide activates three receptors, potentially producing a different combination of effects throughout the body.

In a recent development, to investigate what people were experiencing, the researchers used AI to examine nearly 150,000 Reddit posts and comments. They identified approximately 14,000 users who claimed to have personally taken an unapproved version of retatrutide.

Recent findings suggest that the AI systems then extracted descriptions of symptoms that customers associated with the medication and translated those descriptions into standardized medical terminology. This allowed researchers to compare reports even when different people used different words to describe similar experiences.

After excluding expected effects such as weight loss and reduced appetite, the team identified 7,823 consumers who reported at least one symptom that could be medically classified.

In a recent development, "A researcher might be able to examine a few thousand Reddit posts by hand, but looking at nearly 150,000 would be an enormous undertaking," says Sehgal. "AI makes it possible to analyze these conversations at scale, identifying patterns in what people are sharing that would otherwise be difficult to recognize.".

A Surprising Appetite Paradox Emerges.

The most striking difference involved hunger.

In retatrutide's Phase 2 clinical trials (the drug is at the moment in Phase 3 trials, the final step before FDA approval), participants most commonly experienced gastrointestinal complaints, including nausea. These effects are familiar concerns with medications that influence appetite and digestion.

Recent findings suggest that but among Reddit owners who reported taking unapproved retatrutide, the pattern looked different. Increased appetite emerged as the most frequently described classifiable symptom, despite the substantial weight-loss effects demonstrated in clinical testing.

The researchers also compared the upcoming findings with their earlier analysis of semaglutide and tirzepatide.

Compared with those earlier Reddit reports, discussions involving unapproved retatrutide contained proportionally more mentions of appetite-related changes, sleep disturbances, increased heart rate, and muscle-related symptoms. Reports of nausea and other digestive complaints were proportionally less common.

According to recent reports, these differences could reflect how retatrutide interacts with the body. However, they could also result from differences between the groups of people discussing the medications, their other drug use, or the contents of the unapproved products.

"Retatrutide works differently from existing GLP-1 drugs, so it's possible that its effects on the body are different, too," notes Jena Shaw Tronieri, Senior Research Investigator at Penn's Center for Weight and Eating Disorders and a co-author of the study.

Industry observers note that "But the people discussing it on Reddit also may be different," she notes. "People willing to obtain an unapproved medication on the gray market likely differ from other clinical populations. Some may be taking multiple experimental peptides, and we can't verify exactly what they're taking. We need more research to understand what, if anything, these differences in self-reported symptoms mean.".

Can AI Detect Drug Safety Concerns Earlier?

Beyond the findings about retatrutide, the study demonstrates how AI could potentially improve the early detection of drug safety concerns.

Traditional monitoring systems depend heavily on clinical trials, reports submitted to regulators, and information collected by healthcare professionals. People obtaining experimental medications through unapproved channels may not be represented in those systems.

Social media offers another source of information, allowing researchers to identify recurring experiences that might otherwise escape attention. However, these reports must be independently investigated before they can be considered reliable evidence of a drug-related problem.

The Penn team has already seen an example of how this approach can help guide further research.

Industry observers note that in their previous investigation of semaglutide and tirzepatide, researchers identified online reports of menstrual irregularities. Those findings subsequently encouraged another scientific team to examine similar symptoms using the FDA's database of reported adverse drug events.

The follow-up study, published in Obstetrics & Gynecology, also detected disproportionate reports of certain menstrual changes. Although those findings did not establish causation, they provided additional reasons to investigate the potential connection.

The researchers hope their retatrutide findings will lead to similar independent studies, particularly as the drug advances through clinical development.

Recent findings suggest that "That's what we hope will happen with this study," notes Sehgal. "Other researchers can take what we find on Reddit and look for the same patterns in other datasets, using entirely different methods. Whether those signals hold up or not, the goal is to build a better understanding of what people are actually experiencing.".

In a recent development, the research was conducted through the University of Pennsylvania's School of Engineering and Applied Science and Perelman School of Medicine. Benjamin Rader of Boston Children's Hospital also contributed as a co-author. Funding was provided in part by the University of Pennsylvania's Penn Medical Communication Research Institute. Tronieri disclosed receiving an investigator-initiated grant from Novo Nordisk on behalf of the University of Pennsylvania, along with consulting fees from Currax Pharmaceuticals, LLC. No conflicts of interest were reported by the other authors.

#47074. What's the best GTA?

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1348 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eurogamer ↗ Open Full Page

What's the best GTA?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1348 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, as we teeter on the brink of gaming's biggest launch of 2026 - perhaps even decade - so many questions swirl: which GTA 6 cars will make the best vrrrrm?
  • Because I'm old, my journey with the series began all the way back in 1997, with the advent of GTA 1.
  • Vice City is certainly the GTA I've fondest memories of, even if I did mostly play it as a glorified jukebox.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, as we teeter on the brink of gaming's biggest launch of 2026 - perhaps even decade - so many questions swirl: which GTA 6 cars will make the best vrrrrm? Is it possible for me to be any more obsessed with that Justice theme song? On a scale of one to ten, how many dongs? Answers will inevitably come, but for now - as we crank up the Phil Collins and roar deeper into Eurogamer's GTA Week - there's only one question we're concerned with. Yes, it's the return of our irregular series The Big Question, in which we ponder another topical talking point before wafting it lovingly over to you. And this time around we're asking, what's the best GTA?

Because I'm old, my journey with the series began all the way back in 1997, with the advent of GTA 1. I still vividly remember sitting with the included paper map sprawled across my lap, wide-eyed at the top-down sandbox as my hands reckoned with the weird controls. I remember feeling dizzy at the thrill of high-speed freedom (and possibly the antiquated frame rate) as I tore across Liberty City, San Andreas, and Vice City - particularly whenever this catchy little number came on. I was never massively into those early GTAs, though, not even when the series shifted to full 3D with GTA 3. And it wasn't until Vice City's arrival in 2002, that I began to properly appreciate the series' rhythms - even though I'll readily admit I was at my happiest tearing through the streets with the radio blaring. Vice City's soundtrack, from A Flock of Seagulls to Loverboy and everything in between, is still unmatched today.

But is it the best GTA? Vice City is certainly the GTA I've fondest memories of, even if I did mostly play it as a glorified jukebox. And as much as I've a soft spot for Chinatown Wars on Nintendo DS (a game whose propulsive style and classic top-down aesthetic did a fine job of melding GTAs old and newly introduced), Vice City is the GTA I've returned to most. But what about others on the Eurogamer team? I asked, they've answered with their own personal bests, and when they're done yammering, it's over to you - there's even a poll! And don't forget we'll be exploring the series more thoroughly as GTA Week continues.

Industry observers note that I think, even to this day, GTA: Vice City represents what I think the best Grand Theft Auto is. The vibes, even 24 years later, are immaculate: its vision of Miami in the '80's, with all its cocaine-fueled, sun-washed Yuppie excess makes for the perfect backdrop in a game that's all about freedom and fantasy. The first half of Vice City orientates you wonderfully - casting you as Ray Liotta's arrogant, low-key psychopathic Tommy Vercetti - and letting you quietly get to know the rules of this frontier of narcotic hedonism.

Industry observers note that then you're let loose, wide-eyed with nostrils flared, into the second half of the game: a completely open-ended experience that's all about money, moxie, and madness. Take over businesses, build the Vercetti empire, strongarm your way into Vice City's seedy underbelly in any way you see fit. Even in a more nascent form, Rockstar managed to combine open world 'side activities' with its main narrative, building on everything GTA 3 put down without losing sight of the core theme (something I think San Andreas is guilty of; that game goes off the rails by the third island, whereas I think Vice City always keeps its focus quite neat).

With Vice City, it feels like Rockstar was at the peak of its power, the excesses of its neon-soaked in-game world reflected in the developer's ambitions in the real one: Ray Liotta, Burt Reynolds, Tom Sizemore, Luis Guzmán, Gary Busey, Danny Trejo, Debbie Harry, Danny Dyer, Philip Michael Thomas, William Fichtner… that is an absolutely ridiculous cast, and - in researching the game for something else I'm writing - I have learned there was so much on-set tension between this uncontrollable star power and Rockstar's development team that Reynolds nearly had a fistfight with studio co-founder Dan Houser.

That tension, and that slightly arrogant ambition on behalf of Rockstar, manifest in the bones of Vice City. It's a game struggling against its confines, made by a developer feeling like there is nothing in the world that can stop them. I imagine GTA 6 may feel the same, so how fitting, then, that we're going back to Vice City for the pleasure of it.

Barring the original, Vice City was the GTA I played longest, so those are the cornerstones of my GTA experiences. But San Andreas left the biggest impression on me. And I think it's because it was the first game I played that really attempted to portray Black culture, albeit through a stereotyped and potentially problematic West Coast rap lens' - I don't know how well it holds up today.

Sources indicate that I was very into West Coast rap and hip-hop at the time, and the idea I could partially experience the lives which were referenced in that music so frequently - that I could live a kind of NWA origin story through the character CJ - really appealed to me, as it obviously did to many other people. It felt like I was coming straight outta Compton, as it were. It was rap tourism, which was probably totally fake and insincere to the actual experience of a life like that, but I drank it up all the same.

Fast-forward to GTA 5, which I think of as San Andreas mark two (in a similar way that I think of GTA 6 as Vice City mark two), and it's still startlingly apparent upon playing it - even now, many years after it was first released - that no other tech giant attempts Black culture in the same way. No one even dares. And while I'm totally not the right person to evaluate how well Rockstar carries it off, it does make the GTA experience unique.

Back to San Andreas and I also enjoyed its ridiculous bloat: the gym sessions, the mini-games, eating burgers. It was like living a life in that sunny city, a life I couldn't live otherwise. I'm excited that some of those features are making their way back into GTA 6.

I've never visited America, but I've never been more fond of any city in the world than Latest York. It may not have been called that in GTA 4, but it is the closest any game has got to making me realise my dream of living in and exploring the city.

Sources indicate that GTA 4's Liberty City has one of my favourite aesthetics in games: the dreary, autumnal look where the most sunshine you get is an overcast day. Perhaps Latest York's relatively compact layout (compared to sprawling Los Angeles) is what made it possible to replicate most of its boroughs in-game, and what helped it achieve a sense of place no other GTA comes close to. I knew my way around so much of that map just by landmarks. I was surprised how much of the area around Niko's house I remember when I revisited the game five-ish years ago.

In a recent development, I also consider GTA 4 to be the last entry in the series' classic era. Despite being the first to use Rockstar's now-standard RAGE engine, its controls were just about as loose and arcadey as its 3D predecessors. RAGE's weighty animations gave its characters and cars the look and motion of their real-life counterparts without interfering too much with how they felt to control. GTA 4 stood on the boundary of old and fresh while delivering the series' next evolution - a tough act for any sequel to follow.

According to recent reports, so that's The Big Question, and the best - or at least our favourite - GTAs... now it's over to you!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A group of elderly residents at a retirement home in France have been introduced GTA 6, and some are already hoping to get their hands on the game for Christmas.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A group of elderly residents at a retirement home in France have been introduced GTA 6, and some are already hoping to get their hands on the game for Christmas.

Rockstar Games’ highly anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6 finally launched on November 19, 2026, more than 13 years after the release of GTA 5.

In a recent development, the open-world crime game has attracted enormous attention worldwide, with fans taking time off work to play it. According to French broadcaster TF1, requests for annual leave in France increased by 8% around the game’s launch. Now, the game has been introduced to the older generations.

On November 20, residents at the Domitys senior living facility in Serris, Seine-et-Marne, were introduced to GTA 6 as part of an organized gaming session.

As reported by ICI Paris Île-de-France, the residents swapped their usual activities for an opportunity to explore the game’s virtual world, with many particularly enjoying its boat-driving sequences.

Sources indicate that 82-year-old Jacqueline was among the most enthusiastic participants, successfully collecting two packages of cocaine during a mission. “I had never touched a controller before 9am this morning. And by 2:30pm, I was fishing out two packages of drugs,” she joked.

Another resident, 86-year-old Lucienne, was equally impressed by the game’s visuals, describing them as incredible and comparing the experience to watching a real film.

Meanwhile, 75-year-old Yvan admitted that the controls were difficult to master, joking that he was no longer 20 and struggled to keep up with the action.

Staff explained that the residents had found driving and shooting particularly challenging, but enjoyed exploring the environment by boat.

The experience proved popular enough that Lucienne stated she intended to ask her children for GTA 6 for Christmas, while Jacqueline suggested installing a console in the communal lounge.

Police can’t wait for GTA 6 to be released so they can “catch a break”.
