SNL’s ‘Sister’ sketch hit a nerve, but here’s how to care for elderly parents without upending your life

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3123 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In its 50 years on the air, Saturday Night Live has tackled more than its fair share of social issues.
  • According to recent reports, in its 50 years on the air, Saturday Night Live has tackled more than its fair share of social issues.
  • According to recent reports, this sketch, starring host-for-the-night John Mulaney, promotes Sister™ as the solution to caring for aging parents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In its 50 years on the air, Saturday Night Live has tackled more than its fair share of social issues. But rarely has an SNL sketch resonated as deeply—and prompted as many national conversations—as the Sister commercial parody that aired on November 14, 2026. This sketch, starring host-for-the-night John Mulaney, promotes Sister™ as the solution to caring for aging parents. The parody claims that simply texting the words “Dad fell” to your sister will prompt her to quit her job, break her lease, and completely upend her life to come take care of him—for free. Clearly, the all-male writing team of Streeter Seidell (who dedicated the sketch to his sister, Heidi), Mikey Day, Simon Rich, and Chase Rosenberg are onto something. AARP found that as of 2025, 59 million Americans were providing care for an adult loved one, and women made up 61% of those caregivers. And it’s taking a toll. AARP reports that caregivers of adults over 50 have been caregiving for 5 years and spend 26 hours per week providing care—up from an average of 3.9 years and 22 hours per week as of 2020. About 20% of those caregivers rate themselves as having fair or poor health, and they report an average of 7 poor mental health days per month. These unpaid caregivers spend an average of $11,508 per year on caretaking, which is equal to 31% of the median household income. Women across the country may have laughed through their rage at this painfully accurate comedy—but they deserve more than the mere satisfaction of simply feeling seen by an incisive satire. Cameron Huddleston, author of Mom and Dad, We Need to Talk, and Dr. Darla Bishop, financial wellness expert, public health researcher, and author of How to Afford Everything, offer the following practical suggestions for how America’s siblings can take care of aging parents without upending their lives, bankrupting themselves, or emptying their retirement accounts. Don’t minimize the costs of caregiving The humor of the SNL sketch relies on the family’s ignoring and downplaying the very real cost the sister pays when she becomes the caregiver. As Dr. Bishop puts it, “If you’re cutting back your hours, turning down promotions, or dipping into your retirement savings, caregiving has a price tag, even when no money changes hands.” But the sister faces more than just financial costs. We see her clash with her father and brother and argue with her husband. “In my work, I teach people to think about their three currencies: time, energy, and money,” Dr. Bishop notes. “Caregiving requires all three.” So rather than the sister being a free resource, as Mulaney claims in the ad, she’s using up all of her currencies while her brother pays nothing. Recognizing the heavy costs of caregiving is the first step to breaking the dynamic illustrated by SNL. “I want families to understand that just because you can afford to help your parents today doesn’t mean you can afford the long-term consequences of doing it alone,” Dr. Bishop says. Don’t ignore available resources “When a parent needs care, families assume they have two choices: do it themselves or pay someone else,” Dr. Bishop says. “But there are resources in between, and finding them could save your family thousands of dollars and countless hours.” Specifically, Dr. Bishop recommends starting with your local Area Agency on Aging, which can help you find services like transportation, meal delivery, respite care, and caregiver support. She also suggests exploring the Eldercare Locator at eldercare.acl.gov to help find affordable caregiving near you. You also don’t have to figure out these services on your own. According to Huddleston, an aging life care professional can help. (These people were previously known as geriatric care managers.) “These professionals will be familiar with resources in your area—from adult day care centers to government programs and community assistance,” Huddleston says. To find an aging life care professional, check out the Aging Life Care Association in your area. And don’t forget other, potentially overlooked resources available to you. Your parents may be eligible for Medicaid, depending on their income, health, and location. The VA’s Aid and Attendance program provides benefits for veterans and their spouses that help cover the cost of assistance with activities of daily living. Even your own employer benefits may help. “Some workplaces offer caregiver support, flexible scheduling, or access to care coordinators,” Dr. Bishop says. Don’t go it alone Huddleston was a caregiver for her mom, who had Alzheimer’s disease. One of her regrets about that time was not asking for more help from her family. “If I had asked, I would’ve gotten more help,” she says, “but I didn’t want to be a burden on others.” This gets to a common mindset the SNL skit illustrates: A lot of women are afraid to ask for help. “We assume it’s our responsibility, and we don’t want to appear like we can’t manage that responsibility,” Huddleston says. While it’s true that sometimes women ask for help and don’t receive it, Huddleston believes that many families assume the caregiver has it covered. “My husband was great about helping with my mom, doing so much to support me and her,” she says. “I’d love to see more men respond that way. But if they’re not seeing the toll it takes on the caregiver, as my husband saw daily with me, they probably aren’t even aware of how much of a sacrifice it is to care for a parent.” When asking for help, Dr. Bishop’s three currencies framework can help you figure out who can do what. You can divide responsibilities based on the time, energy, and money you each bring to the table. “Maybe one sibling lives nearby and can take Mom to appointments while another has more financial flexibility and can contribute toward paid care,” Dr. Bishop suggests. “A third might be great at managing paperwork, coordinating benefits, or researching resources.” Huddleston recommends keeping a running list of the types of support you need so that you’re prepared to make specific requests. “You might ask your brother to find an aging life care professional and cover the cost, to line up a housekeeper or lawn maintenance for your parents’ house, to pay for grocery delivery, to come stay with your parent in the evenings or weekends to give you a break,” she says. She also wants caregivers to let go of any guilt they have about asking for specific help. “It would be easier if men stepped up without being asked to help,” she says. “But if you’re not getting the help you need, don’t feel bad about asking for it.” Don’t wait to make decisions It’s easy to put off thinking about Mom and Dad’s health. None of us like to consider our parents’ mortality, and the idea of losing independence can be terrifying to an aging parent. But it’s easier to make good decisions before Dad falls, when no one is panicked or stressed. That’s why both Huddleston and Dr. Bishop both recommend having a family meeting well before there’s a crisis. “Put everything on the table,” Dr. Bishop says. “Ask yourselves, ‘What does our parent need? What resources do they already have? What can each of us realistically contribute without jeopardizing our own financial security?’” If your family tends to avoid such conversations, Huddleston suggests using the SNL skit as a jumping-off point to start the conversation. Don’t neglect your own long-term care planning Another way to break the cycle of relying on women’s unpaid caregiving is by planning for our own future care needs—and much earlier than you might think. “By the time you’re 50 years old, you should be thinking about long-term care and how you could pay for professional care so that you don’t have to rely entirely on a family member for support,” Huddleston says. “At that age (and into your early 60s if you’re healthy), you can still qualify for long-term care insurance or a hybrid life insurance policy with long-term care benefits.” Dr. Bishop also recommends getting your affairs in order—and that doesn’t just mean having a will in place. “One of the greatest gifts you can give your adult children is not making them play detective during a family crisis,” she says. Specifically, your kids should know where to find your vital documents, who manages your money, what insurance you have, and your wishes in the event that you can’t make medical or financial decisions for yourself. So funny it hurts It’s unlikely that Saturday Night Live expected its three-minute parody to trigger a national reckoning about women’s disproportionate caregiving burden. But it struck a nerve for a very good reason. As Dr. Bishop puts it, “women aren’t the backup plan. We are THE PLAN.” But that doesn’t mean we’re stuck with this dynamic forever. We can end our reliance on women’s unpaid labor by recognizing the heavy time, energy, and money cost of caregiving; exploring all available resources; refusing to let one person handle all caregiving; making proactive decisions; and planning ahead for our own long-term care needs. “The answer isn’t for women to stop caring about their families,” Dr. Bishop says. “It’s for families to stop assuming that caring automatically equals sacrificing your career, your finances, or your own well-being.”.

According to recent reports, you also don’t have to figure out these services on your own. According to Huddleston, an aging life care professional can help. (These people were previously known as geriatric care managers.).

According to recent reports, “These professionals will be familiar with resources in your area—from adult day care centers to government programs and community assistance,” Huddleston indicates. To find an aging life care professional, check out the Aging Life Care Association in your area.

And don’t forget other, potentially overlooked resources available to you. Your parents may be eligible for Medicaid, depending on their income, health, and location. The VA’s Aid and Attendance program provides benefits for veterans and their spouses that help cover the cost of assistance with activities of daily living. Even your own employer benefits may help.

According to recent reports, “Some workplaces offer caregiver support, flexible scheduling, or access to care coordinators,” Dr. Bishop says.

Huddleston was a caregiver for her mom, who had Alzheimer’s disease. One of her regrets about that time was not asking for more help from her family.

“If I had asked, I would’ve gotten more help,” she claims, “but I didn’t want to be a burden on others.” This gets to a common mindset the SNL skit illustrates: A lot of women are afraid to ask for help. “We assume it’s our responsibility, and we don’t want to appear like we can’t manage that responsibility,” Huddleston says.

While it’s true that sometimes women ask for help and don’t receive it, Huddleston believes that many families assume the caregiver has it covered.

“My husband was great about helping with my mom, doing so much to support me and her,” she states. “I’d love to see more men respond that way. But if they’re not seeing the toll it takes on the caregiver, as my husband saw daily with me, they probably aren’t even aware of how much of a sacrifice it is to care for a parent.”.

Sources indicate that when asking for help, Dr. Bishop’s three currencies framework can help you figure out who can do what. You can divide responsibilities based on the time, energy, and money you each bring to the table.

Industry observers note that “Maybe one sibling lives nearby and can take Mom to appointments while another has more financial flexibility and can contribute toward paid care,” Dr. Bishop suggests. “A third might be great at managing paperwork, coordinating benefits, or researching resources.”.

Huddleston recommends keeping a running list of the types of support you need so that you’re prepared to make specific requests. “You might ask your brother to find an aging life care professional and cover the cost, to line up a housekeeper or lawn maintenance for your parents’ house, to pay for grocery delivery, to come stay with your parent in the evenings or weekends to give you a break,” she states.

According to recent reports, she also wants caregivers to let go of any guilt they have about asking for specific help. “It would be easier if men stepped up without being asked to help,” she indicates. “But if you’re not getting the help you need, don’t feel bad about asking for it.”.

It’s easy to put off thinking about Mom and Dad’s health. None of us like to consider our parents’ mortality, and the idea of losing independence can be terrifying to an aging parent. But it’s easier to make good decisions before Dad falls, when no one is panicked or stressed. That’s why both Huddleston and Dr. Bishop both recommend having a family meeting well before there’s a crisis.

Recent findings suggest that “Put everything on the table,” Dr. Bishop notes. “Ask yourselves, ‘What does our parent need? What resources do they already have? What can each of us realistically contribute without jeopardizing our own financial security?’”.

If your family tends to avoid such conversations, Huddleston suggests using the SNL skit as a jumping-off point to start the conversation.

Another way to break the cycle of relying on women’s unpaid caregiving is by planning for our own future care needs—and much earlier than you might think.

“By the time you’re 50 years old, you should be thinking about long-term care and how you could pay for professional care so that you don’t have to rely entirely on a family member for support,” Huddleston states. “At that age (and into your early 60s if you’re healthy), you can still qualify for long-term care insurance or a hybrid life insurance policy with long-term care benefits.”.

Dr. Bishop also recommends getting your affairs in order—and that doesn’t just mean having a will in place. “One of the greatest gifts you can give your adult children is not making them play detective during a family crisis,” she claims.

Specifically, your kids should know where to find your crucial documents, who manages your money, what insurance you have, and your wishes in the event that you can’t make medical or financial decisions for yourself.

It has been revealed that it’s unlikely that Saturday Night Live expected its three-minute parody to trigger a national reckoning about women’s disproportionate caregiving burden. But it struck a nerve for a very good reason.

As Dr. Bishop puts it, “women aren’t the backup strategy. We are THE PLAN.”.

But that doesn’t mean we’re stuck with this dynamic forever. We can end our reliance on women’s unpaid labor by recognizing the heavy time, energy, and money cost of caregiving; exploring all available resources; refusing to let one person handle all caregiving; making proactive decisions; and planning ahead for our own long-term care needs.

According to recent reports, “The answer isn’t for women to stop caring about their families,” Dr. Bishop notes. “It’s for families to stop assuming that caring automatically equals sacrificing your career, your finances, or your own well-being.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, south Korea used emergency disaster alerts during its national college admission test to catch prohibited devices.
  • Sources indicate that the College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), also known as Suneung, is one of South Korea’s most key yearly events.
  • Industry observers note that the brutal exam, held every third Thursday of November, lasts eight hours, from 8:40 AM to 5:45 PM, often being the deciding factor for the trajectory of the students’ lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, south Korea used emergency disaster alerts during its national college admission test to catch prohibited devices. The anti-cheating measure was announced after a cheater in South Korea’s tax accountant exam confessed to using AI and a micro-camera to cheat. The alerts caught a total of 54 candidates, with 111 total when combined with other means, The Korean Herald reports.

Sources indicate that the College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), also known as Suneung, is one of South Korea’s most key yearly events. The exam is so significant that the whole country pauses and makes way for the test-takers; police clear the roads and escort late students, noisy construction and maintenance are suspended, aircraft are grounded, military exercises are paused, and the stock market opens an hour later. The government even requests public institutions and private companies start work later, delaying the rush hour and ensuring the students arrive unimpeded.

Industry observers note that the brutal exam, held every third Thursday of November, lasts eight hours, from 8:40 AM to 5:45 PM, often being the deciding factor for the trajectory of the students’ lives. With such high stakes, cheating is not unusual.

In a recent development, the month before the CSAT, South Korea’s Certified Tax Accountant exam received an unusually large number of high scorers — with 66 candidates scoring over 90+ in introductory accounting over only two in 2025 and one in 2024, as reported by The Korean Herald. The top scorer, Han Won-seok, confessed to cheating on his lawyer’s YouTube channel, admitting to cheating using a micro-camera that feeds images of the test to an AI on his smartphone.

The confession went live days before the Suneung, prompting the South Korean government to tighten up its anti-cheating measures for the exam, with Prime Minister Lee Jae Myung stating, "Cheating involving the abuse of AI in South Korea, where public examinations significantly affect the distribution of opportunities and resources, rocks the basic order of our society by undermining fairness and trust," calling for an overhaul of the system to address AI-assisted cheating, as reported by Yonhap News Agency.

Industry observers note that the first alert rang at 8:30 AM, ten minutes before the exam started, catching 31 students with unauthorized devices, whose scores were immediately invalidated despite the test not having started yet. The next two alerts at 2:21 and 2:57 PM caught 23 more, bringing the total to 54. As of today, Yonhap News Agency reports that 111 total students were caught with unauthorized devices — 52 were caught through other methods such as metal detectors, WiFi signal detection, and physical inspections, with a further five caught red-handed using prohibited devices.

According to recent reports, alongside the South Korean government’s reaction to the confession, a law school entrance exam candidate accused of AI-assisted cheating like Han Won-seok had died on the day of the Suneung. In July, Lee Jin-woo, a Legal Education Eligibility Test (LEET) candidate, achieved an impressive perfect score and is reportedly the first to do so. Months later, he published a book about his study methods, talking about lifestyle changes, exercise, diet, and even reduced smartphone use.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

When the tax accountant cheater confessed on Sunday, it led to online suspicion about Lee’s perfect LEET score, with two lawyers even filing legal complaints accusing him of obstruction of official duties. Lee was supposed to be interviewed on YouTube early on Thursday to prove his academic abilities, but he did not show up. Later that day, when Police investigated the legal complaints and after he was reported missing, he was found dead of cardiac arrest at 1:12 PM in a motel, with a note at the scene stating he was mentally and physically exhausted, with no mention of the cheating allegations, as reported by Yonhap News Agency.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, apple has received much criticism for being late to the AI game.
  • In a recent development, apple has received much criticism for being late to the AI game.
  • Though the initial capabilities of Apple Intelligence were rather lackluster compared with its peers, Apple spent the next two years rapidly refining its offerings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, apple has received much criticism for being late to the AI game. While OpenAI helped define the AI boom beginning in late 2021, and Google and other tech giants quickly jumped on the AI train the following year, Apple didn’t make its first real foray into artificial intelligence until 2024 with Apple Intelligence. Though the initial capabilities of Apple Intelligence were rather lackluster compared with its peers, Apple spent the next two years rapidly refining its offerings. In 2026, Apple made its AI system much more capable and expansive by introducing more advanced AI tools, including the Siri AI chatbot and Audio Intelligence. And just last month, Apple also debuted an additional AI tool dubbed “intelligent assistant.” The thing is, Apple now has so many AI offerings that it’s getting hard for the average consumer to keep track of what each one does, which devices support which AI tool, and which tools require a fee to access. So, here’s a cheat sheet for making sense of Apple’s increasingly confusing AI lineup. Apple Intelligence Apple Intelligence is the oldest of the company’s modern AI offerings, introduced in 2024. Think of Apple Intelligence as the foundational artificial intelligence layer integrated into Apple’s operating systems, including iOS, macOS, and watchOS. Apple Intelligence includes a suite of smaller AI tools tailored to specific tasks. For example, Apple Intelligence powers Visual Intelligence, which lets Apple’s AI see and understand what’s on your screen or through your camera and take action on it; for example, it can tell you the nutritional information of the food on your plate. Apple Intelligence powers Audio Intelligence, a tool that can help you identify sounds and music and even recap your spoken conversations on some Apple Watches. It is also the engine behind numerous other AI features across your Apple products, including image generation, live translation, select photo editing tools, message summaries, and more. Not every device that supports Apple Intelligence supports all its features. Any Mac with an Apple Silicon chip will run Apple Intelligence, but you’ll need a Mac with an M3 chip and 12 GB of RAM or more to use some of its most advanced features, including custom Siri Voices and advanced AI dictation. For the iPhone, you’ll need an iPhone 17 Pro or later to use those advanced Apple Intelligence features (iPhone 15 Pro and later is required for most Apple Intelligence features). As for Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch, that’s limited to the upcoming Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Series 4. Siri AI Siri AI is Apple’s new chatbot. Though people often use the terms “Siri AI” and “Apple Intelligence” interchangeably, they are actually distinct. Apple Intelligence is the foundational AI system integrated into Apple’s operating systems. Siri AI is the natural-language gateway to Apple Intelligence—it lets you communicate as you would with a person to give it commands or find information, which it then carries out using Apple Intelligence’s capabilities. Siri AI runs on the cloud on any device that supports iOS 27, macOS 27, iPadOS 27, visionOS 27, watchOS 27, and (soon) tvOS 27. However, if you want to run some aspects of Siri AI locally on your device, you’ll need a Mac with an M3 chip and 12GB of RAM or more, or an iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone Air, or later. Intelligent Assistant This is Apple’s newest major artificial intelligence tool, the most impressive, and the one that most muddies Apple’s AI branding. “Intelligent assistant,” introduced last month and released this month as part of the updated Logic Pro, Pages, Numbers, and Keynote apps in Apple’s paid Creator Studio suite, is a new natural-language AI tool aimed at helping creators be more productive. The tool is integrated into the above apps in the form of a chatbot. There’s a text field where you type instructions to the intelligent assistant (“make this piano track sound like it was recorded in a concert hall” or “fix the formula errors in this spreadsheet”). The changes happen like magic—all very impressive stuff. As a matter of fact, it’s way more impressive than the other capabilities Apple has shown off for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. So why hasn’t Apple branded these new AI features as Apple Intelligence? The answer: Intelligent assistant is not powered by Apple Intelligence or Siri AI. Instead, the new AI tools use Apple Foundation Models combined with additional models from third-party providers, in this case, OpenAI and Google. This explains why intelligent assistant is so capable (both OpenAI and Google have a huge lead over Apple in the AI space) and also why Apple has eschewed the Apple Intelligence branding for the work it carries out. Does Apple charge for AI? This is where things get really muddied for people. Apple’s AI pricing runs from free, to a monthly subscription fee, to higher usage limits with select iCloud Plus plans. Presently, using Apple Intelligence and Siri AI is free for all people. However, Apple says this won’t last. With the release of the 27.3 versions of its operating systems in December, customers will have daily limits when using Siri AI and Apple Intelligence. If they exceed those limits, they won’t be able to use any Apple Intelligence features that require cloud processing (which costs Apple compute power). If users do want higher Apple Intelligence and Siri AI limits, they can get more by paying for an iCloud Plus blueprint (if they don’t already have one). The 50GB iCloud Plus plan, which costs just 99 cents per month, doesn’t increase your AI limits. However, the other iCloud Plus plans do: 200GB ($2.99 per month): 2x limit increase 2TB ($9.99 per month): 5x limit increase 6TB ($29.99 per month): 10x limit increase 12TB ($59.99 per month): 20x limit increase As for intelligent assistant access in Logic Pro, Pages, Keynote, and Numbers, users already need to pony up. Intelligent assistant is available only as part of Apple’s Creator Studio subscription bundle, for which it charges $12.99 per month or $129 per year. This means that if you want as much access as possible to Apple’s AI offerings, you’ll need to subscribe to two subscription plans.

Housing market shift: 76 metros where home prices are falling

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1773 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that want more housing market stories from Lance Lambert’s ResiClub in your inbox?
  • Want more housing market stories from Lance Lambert’s ResiClub in your inbox?
  • Sources indicate that based on ResiClub’s analysis of the Zillow Home Value Index, nationally aggregated U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that want more housing market stories from Lance Lambert’s ResiClub in your inbox? Subscribe to the ResiClub newsletter. Based on ResiClub’s analysis of the Zillow Home Value Index, nationally aggregated U.S. home prices rose 0.7% year over year from October 2025 to October 2026. That marks another month-over-month deceleration, down from the 1.0% year-over-year increase from September 2025 to September 2026 and the 1.3% year-over-year increase from August 2025 to August 2026. After contracting over the past year, the number of America’s major regional housing markets seeing year-over-year declines is rising again, as the already soft national housing market (which is still amid the multiyear post-boom cyclical cooling window) sees another burst of softening amid the recent run-up in long-term yields and mortgage rates. —> 54 of the nation’s 300 largest housing markets (i.e., 18% of markets) had a falling year-over-year home price reading in the August 2025 to August 2026 window. —> 66 of the nation’s 300 largest housing markets (i.e., 22% of markets) had a falling year-over-year home price reading in the September 2025 to September 2026 window. —> 76 of the nation’s 300 largest housing markets (i.e., 25% of markets) had a falling year-over-year home price reading in the October 2025 to October 2026 window. We should point out that the nationally aggregated housing market is softer than the counts above suggest, given that year-over-year home price declines are currently skewed slightly toward larger metro areas. Home prices are still climbing a tad nominally (not inflation-adjusted) year over year in some pockets where active inventory remains well below pre-pandemic 2019 levels, such as certain areas in the Northeast and Midwest. In contrast, some pockets in states like Texas, Florida, Washington, and Colorado—where active inventory exceeds pre-pandemic 2019 levels by a solid clip—are seeing either material corrections, modest home price pullbacks, or simply flat pricing. Looking ahead, the big question is how much of a burst of softening the nationally aggregated housing market will see, now that the 30-year fixed-mortgage rate has jumped back above 7.0% amid an already strained affordability environment and the still ongoing post-boom cyclical cooling period. To keep an eye on it, ResiClub recommends closely monitoring local active inventory/months of supply over the next several months. Click here for an interactive version of the chart below. Many of the housing markets seeing the most softness, where homebuyers have gained the most leverage since the pandemic housing boom fizzled out, are primarily located in Sunbelt regions or the Mountain West. Many of these areas saw even greater price surges during the pandemic housing boom, with home price growth outpacing local income levels. As pandemic-driven domestic migration slowed and mortgage rates rose in 2022, markets like Tampa, Florida, and Austin faced challenges, relying on local income levels to support frothy home prices. That Sunbelt softening was further compounded by an abundance of upcoming-home supply in the Sunbelt. Builders are often willing to lower prices or offer affordability incentives to maintain sales, which also has a cooling effect on the resale market. As a result, some buyers who might have previously opted for existing homes are instead choosing new construction with more attractive deals—which added further upward pressure to resale inventory growth over the past few years. Of course, while 76 of the nation’s 300 largest metro-area housing markets are seeing year-over-year home price declines, another 224 are seeing year-over-year home price increases. However, most of the places posting “nominal gains” are seeing gains below income growth and consumer price growth, which economists call “real” (inflation-adjusted) home price declines. Where are home prices still up on a year-over-year basis? See the map below. Below is a historical chart showing the year-over-year change in home prices across the 50 largest metro housing markets, with the yellow line representing the national aggregate, dating back to 2000. While the range [see chart above] between the strongest and weakest metro-area housing markets right now is fairly normal historically speaking, the bifurcation (i.e., direction) itself—the share of markets with rising home prices versus those with falling prices—is wider than normal, given that national appreciation is in a softer market with growth barely above 0.0%. And the longer some markets remain in the “rising” camp while others stay in the “falling” camp, the wider the gulf can become between the relatively more resilient markets and the weaker ones. For example, home prices in the Hartford, Conneticut, metro area are now 28.0% above their 2022 peak, while home prices in the Austin metro area sit 28.8% below their 2022 peak. Some of that bifurcation boils down to mean reversion, with many of the outright home price declines occurring in markets that overheated further during the pandemic housing boom. Note: For the historical chart below, we analyzed the 200 largest markets rather than the 300 used above, as some markets ranked 201 to 300 lack complete data going back to 2000. When weighted by population (not visualized), the housing market appears slightly weaker than the chart below suggests—which aligns with the fact that among just the 50 largest housing markets, 21 (42%) are currently posting negative year-over-year price growth, and nationally aggregated home prices are up just 0.7% year over year using the Zillow Home Value Index.

Sources indicate that based on ResiClub’s analysis of the Zillow Home Value Index, nationally aggregated U.S. home prices rose 0.7% year over year from October 2025 to October 2026. That marks another month-over-month deceleration, down from the 1.0% year-over-year increase from September 2025 to September 2026 and the 1.3% year-over-year increase from August 2025 to August 2026.

After contracting over the past year, the number of America’s major regional housing markets seeing year-over-year declines is rising again, as the already soft national housing market (which is still amid the multiyear post-boom cyclical cooling window) sees another burst of softening amid the recent run-up in long-term yields and mortgage rates.

—> 54 of the nation’s 300 largest housing markets (i.e., 18% of markets) had a falling year-over-year home price reading in the August 2025 to August 2026 window.

—> 66 of the nation’s 300 largest housing markets (i.e., 22% of markets) had a falling year-over-year home price reading in the September 2025 to September 2026 window.

—> 76 of the nation’s 300 largest housing markets (i.e., 25% of markets) had a falling year-over-year home price reading in the October 2025 to October 2026 window.

We should point out that the nationally aggregated housing market is softer than the counts above suggest, given that year-over-year home price declines are at the moment skewed slightly toward larger metro areas.

Home prices are still climbing a tad nominally (not inflation-adjusted) year over year in some pockets where active inventory remains well below pre-pandemic 2019 levels, such as certain areas in the Northeast and Midwest. In contrast, some pockets in states like Texas, Florida, Washington, and Colorado—where active inventory exceeds pre-pandemic 2019 levels by a solid clip—are seeing either material corrections, modest home price pullbacks, or simply flat pricing.

Sources indicate that looking ahead, the big question is how much of a burst of softening the nationally aggregated housing market will see, now that the 30-year fixed-mortgage rate has jumped back above 7.0% amid an already strained affordability environment and the still ongoing post-boom cyclical cooling period. To keep an eye on it, ResiClub recommends closely monitoring local active inventory/months of supply over the next several months.

It has been revealed that many of the housing markets seeing the most softness, where homebuyers have gained the most leverage since the pandemic housing boom fizzled out, are primarily located in Sunbelt regions or the Mountain West. Many of these areas saw even greater price surges during the pandemic housing boom, with home price growth outpacing local income levels. As pandemic-driven domestic migration slowed and mortgage rates rose in 2022, markets like Tampa, Florida, and Austin faced challenges, relying on local income levels to support frothy home prices.

That Sunbelt softening was further compounded by an abundance of new-home supply in the Sunbelt. Builders are often willing to lower prices or offer affordability incentives to maintain sales, which also has a cooling effect on the resale market. As a result, some buyers who might have previously opted for existing homes are instead choosing new construction with more attractive deals—which added further upward pressure to resale inventory growth over the past few years.

Motorola’s upcoming Razr Flex foldable is expected to have the same wide foldable form factor as Galaxy Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo, and upcoming leaks not only reveal its design, but hint at some key specs.

Sources indicate that ahead of its supposed 2027 debut, the Motorola Razr Flex has now leaked in a real-life image. The image demonstrates the back of the phone with a dual-camera setup, Pixel-like camera bar, and a design that matches that short and stout look of Galaxy Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo. It also pretty clearly lines up with past teasers of this device.

Rumor has it that the Razr Flex will be even smaller than Samsung or Apple’s wide foldables, and the proportions of this image make that all the more certain.

Beyond this, some regulatory leaks reveal key specs on the Motorola Razr Flex.

The foldable will apparently run Android 17 out of the box – an revision that Razr Fold is only getting just now – and run on the Qualcomm SM8845 Pro chipset. Android Authority notes that this isn’t a chip that’s been announced yet, but it’s thought to be called “Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 Pro.”.

Other rumored specs include a 4.97-inch outer display, 6.92-inch inner display, 5,000 mAh battery, 12GB of RAM, and two 50MP cameras around back. Based on information from a past leak, the color variant pictured above is likely called “Coriander.”.

#47020. Canva added an AI ‘kill switch’ to its tools

Canva added an AI ‘kill switch’ to its tools

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1496 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that over the last few years, Canva, the Australian design platform, has been stuffing generative AI into its products.
  • Over the last few years, Canva, the Australian design platform, has been stuffing generative AI into its products.
  • The first button seems like pure theater to me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that over the last few years, Canva, the Australian design platform, has been stuffing generative AI into its products. Now, it’s giving you the option to make those AI features disappear. On Thursday, the company announced two latest switches to rein in its AI for anyone on Canva Free and Canva Pro. One toggle button hides its generative AI features. Another one will make Canva show less AI-generated material in its library of templates and graphics. The first button seems like pure theater to me. If a user doesn’t want to use AI tools, it’s easy enough to figure out how: Don’t press the sparkly AI button. The second one is more useful, however, since it can help consumers avoid being drowned by AI-generated material while browsing the Canva libraries that made this suite popular in the first place. It’s worth noting that the switch doesn’t ban all AI-generated material from view—it just demonstrates less. [Image: Canva] Both switches are buried in two settings menus. The general AI “kill switch” lives under Profile > Settings > Permissions. Flip it off, and Canva’s generative features are “hidden across Canva,” the company said in an announcement. These include Magic Expand, which extends a photo, and Canva Craft, the first generative image model developed by the company. You can turn them back on whenever you like. Still, Canva hasn’t erased every AI thingamajig. The suite’s AI-based Background Remover and Magic Grab—which picks an object out of a picture to move it somewhere else in the design—are “assistive editing tools,” and therefore are still accessed after toggling AI off. The second control sits under Profile > Your Account > AI Personalization (more on this later). Turn it on, and Canva cuts back the AI-generated material that pops up in search results and recommendations, pushing more human-made stuff to the top. The company claims its AI content is only “a small portion” of its library, like abstract backgrounds and illustrated graphics. [Image: Canva] Why, really The filter matters to people who don’t want to wade through a river full of generative AI creations. It also benefits the humans behind the designs. Canva pays actual humans each time someone uses their work in a design. In theory, that steers money toward the designers and illustrators who fill the Canva library. These features are essentially a temperature check on AI. Canva tied the launch to the public mood, citing Pew Research Center figures: Roughly 6 in 10 Americans say they want more control over how artificial intelligence is used in their lives. “We believe the future of creativity should be defined by choice, not dictated by technology,” the company said in a statement. In an email, Canva says it is “always listening to our community and looking for ways to make Canva work better for them. We’ve heard that people want more choice over AI, and these controls are one way we’re responding. . . . These controls give people more choice over how AI fits into their Canva experience.” But if Canva really wanted to make this happen, why bury the controls? If you want to empower your users and creators, there’s no reason to hide the settings. Rather, you should add the switches right there on the main interface so that people can choose their experience with ease. The company says that putting clearly visible AI kill switches right on the main interface, for every user to see right away, is something they are “actually exploring.” Perhaps Canva fears that too many people will choose to deactivate these features, cutting off one of its revenue streams. After all, in the same announcement, Canva said that its community has used its AI tools more than 38 billion times. The company also says it’s still investing to make its AI wares “even more powerful.” And remember: Canva just built its own generative image model to help shave the costs of so many people using its AI tools. AI is still very much a priority for the company. Canva claims that “this isn’t a marketing play” and that it is just a temporary solution: “Our goal was to get a solution live to our community as rapidly as possible, but that doesn’t mean this is its final form. While it’s early, the response is telling us that people are excited to have this option, but we’ll listen for signals on how it should evolve.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • After a 13-year wait, Rockstar Games’s Grand Theft Auto VI has been released—but for many players, a life of crime isn’t the only appeal.
  • After a 13-year wait, Rockstar Games’s Grand Theft Auto VI has been released—but for many players, a life of crime isn’t the only appeal.
  • The game is set in Leonida (Florida, but fictionalized), and outside Vice City’s limits, the state’s characteristic swamps, waters, and subtropical forests sprawl across the map.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After a 13-year wait, Rockstar Games’s Grand Theft Auto VI has been released—but for many players, a life of crime isn’t the only appeal. The game is set in Leonida (Florida, but fictionalized), and outside Vice City’s limits, the state’s characteristic swamps, waters, and subtropical forests sprawl across the map. Expansive, painstakingly rendered landscapes have long been an integral part of Rockstar’s open-world action-adventure games, including its last major release, Red Dead Redemption 2. As in that title, in GTA VI, the natural world is more than just a backdrop for the main story: Side quests like alligator hunting and a zoologist challenge lead players into the great outdoors. Players have eagerly anticipated the wildlife. A promotional image featuring a lionfish—an invasive species in Florida—sparked hopeful discussion about spear hunting, which is one of the methods used to control their population. Other fans kept running lists of species confirmed ahead of the release date. GTA VI’s birding gameplay and inclusion of 62 avian species has been a particular source of buzz online, and hobbyists are already logging the species they spy on a dedicated website called Leonida Birds. One person said that playing Red Dead Redemption 2 had “flipped the birding switch on,” and that they’ve since identified birds from the game in real life. Perhaps unsurprisingly, research suggests that this deep immersion in video game environments can serve as a valuable way to communicate information about the real natural world, including a study in which RDR2 players correctly identified more photos of wildlife species that had appeared in the game than non-players. “Not sure how GTA VI has suddenly turned me into David Attenborough,” one player remarked on X, “but I just logged off an 8 hour session and immediately want to hop back on to study more birds and wildlife.” In a study published in Geoscience Communication this week, researchers used GTA V’s digital replication of Los Angeles—coupled with data like Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change projections and records of past flooding—to simulate floods caused by sea level rise. Paul Nörenberg, one of the researchers, said in a press release that engaging with these climate effects in a familiar landscape “can bridge a gap in a way that conventional visualizations, such as models or maps, struggle to achieve.” Another study, which interviewed gamers about their experiences, observed that different games allow participants to explore nature through different contexts and perspectives, and games that include environmental destruction “made them contend with exploiting and subjugating nature—both in-game and in the actual world.” Though Grand Theft Auto’s plots are designed to let players explore a life of crime—not climate disaster—the upcoming installment’s gameplay does weave in a range of real-world environmental topics, from animal conservation to chemicals in agriculture. One mission centers on the exotic animal trade; another involves freeing an orca from the Vice City Oceanarium, likely a reference to the now-shuttered Miami Seaquarium, which faced criticism for owning an orca named Lolita that died in captivity in 2023. In a third, a strawberry grower asks the player to visit a meth lab to pick up “discontinued” chemicals that he sprays on his unnaturally large crops, according to an IGN walk-through. This also echoes reality. Driscoll’s, a major agribusiness, faces a class-action lawsuit that alleges the manufacturer sold strawberries contaminated with harmful chemicals without disclosing them. Video game realism does have its limits: The real-life strawberries haven’t turned anyone into giant mutants. Yet.

The game is set in Leonida (Florida, but fictionalized), and outside Vice City’s limits, the state’s characteristic swamps, waters, and subtropical forests sprawl across the map.

Recent findings suggest that expansive, painstakingly rendered landscapes have long been an integral part of Rockstar’s open-world action-adventure games, including its last major release, Red Dead Redemption 2. As in that title, in GTA VI, the natural world is more than just a backdrop for the main story: Side quests like alligator hunting and a zoologist challenge lead players into the great outdoors.

Players have eagerly anticipated the wildlife. A promotional image featuring a lionfish—an invasive species in Florida—sparked hopeful discussion about spear hunting, which is one of the methods used to control their population. Other fans kept running lists of species confirmed ahead of the release date.

It has been revealed that GTA VI’s birding gameplay and inclusion of 62 avian species has been a particular source of buzz online, and hobbyists are already logging the species they spy on a dedicated website called Leonida Birds. One person noted that playing Red Dead Redemption 2 had “flipped the birding switch on,” and that they’ve since identified birds from the game in real life.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, research suggests that this deep immersion in video game environments can serve as a valuable way to communicate information about the real natural world, including a study in which RDR2 players correctly identified more photos of wildlife species that had appeared in the game than non-players.

“Not sure how GTA VI has suddenly turned me into David Attenborough,” one player remarked on X, “but I just logged off an 8 hour session and immediately want to hop back on to study more birds and wildlife.”.

In a study published in Geoscience Communication this week, researchers used GTA V’s digital replication of Los Angeles—coupled with data like Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change projections and records of past flooding—to simulate floods caused by sea level rise.

Paul Nörenberg, one of the researchers, said in a press release that engaging with these climate effects in a familiar landscape “can bridge a gap in a way that conventional visualizations, such as models or maps, struggle to achieve.”.

Another study, which interviewed gamers about their experiences, observed that different games allow participants to explore nature through different contexts and perspectives, and games that include environmental destruction “made them contend with exploiting and subjugating nature—both in-game and in the actual world.”.

One mission centers on the exotic animal trade; another involves freeing an orca from the Vice City Oceanarium, likely a reference to the now-shuttered Miami Seaquarium, which faced criticism for owning an orca named Lolita that died in captivity in 2023.

In a recent development, in a third, a strawberry grower asks the player to visit a meth lab to pick up “discontinued” chemicals that he sprays on his unnaturally large crops, according to an IGN walk-through. This also echoes reality. Driscoll’s, a major agribusiness, faces a class-action lawsuit that alleges the company sold strawberries contaminated with harmful chemicals without disclosing them.

Video game realism does have its limits: The real-life strawberries haven’t turned anyone into giant mutants. Yet.

11 career decisions high performers regret making too late

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 28 min read (5609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~28 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, some career decisions become costly only after too much time has passed.
  • It has been revealed that some career decisions become costly only after too much time has passed.
  • The single decision high performers almost always make too late is firing themselves from day-to-day fulfillment, because their ego is still addicted to being the hero inside the manufacturer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, some career decisions become costly only after too much time has passed. The following insights, from experts in the field, reveal which moves high performers often wish they had made sooner, from protecting their health to asking for help and building stronger networks. These lessons offer clear steps for making better choices before regret sets in. Delegate Authority While Capacity Remains The single decision high performers almost always make too late is firing themselves from day-to-day fulfillment, because their ego is still addicted to being the hero inside the company. When I founded my first Scandinavian fine jewelry brand in Oslo at 22, I built our early momentum by personally touching every single bottleneck: approving every creative cut, negotiating every creator seeding deal, and rewriting campaign copy at 2:00 a.m. Because revenue was climbing and we were landing cultural placements like Khaby Lame and Vogue Scandinavia, I mistook exhaustion for leverage. The turning point came when I realized that by being the best operator in the room, I had capped the company’s valuation at the limit of my personal nervous system. High performers wait until they hit burnout to build standard operating procedures and delegate authority, whereas you actually have to hand off the keys while you still have 40% left in the tank. Once I forced myself to step out of daily order orchestration and document our visual and distribution protocols so the business ran without my fingerprints on every transaction, two things happened: Our enterprise value became transferable (allowing us to close a clean private acquisition exit in Q4 2024), and my own bandwidth opened up to direct film productions. If I could go back, I would have documented and delegated my favorite tasks 12 months earlier, not just the chores I hated. Mommi Live, founder, managing partner & creative director, Mommi Limited Archive Evidence Beyond External Platforms Keeping their track record inside someone else’s platform. High performers usually build their reputation where the work happens: an employer’s system, a marketplace profile, a client’s internal tools. It feels like the record will always be there. Then the job ends, the platform changes its rules, or the old proof simply stops being shown, and years of results are hard to point to. I learned this with my own business. I started selling video editing on Fiverr in 2020, while I was studying computer science. That grew into Mark Studios, which has completed more than 8,000 orders and earned 4,500+ reviews, with a 4.9 rating and Top Rated status. But Fiverr only demonstrates roughly the last two years of reviews, so the visible proof of the early years keeps shrinking even as the total grows. The work was real. The evidence just lived somewhere I didn’t control. What I’d do differently, and what I tell anyone doing great work inside a company or a platform: Keep your own record from day one. Write a short case study after every project that matters, with the problem, what you did, and a measurable result. For a channel whose thumbnails and titles we’ve handled since August 2025, VidIQ revealed views up 30.1% week over week when we captured the stats in May. That number now sits in a case study on my own website instead of only in a client conversation. Ask for testimonials you’re allowed to reuse, and save the numbers while they’re fresh. Your reputation is an asset. Make sure you hold a copy of it. Mark Santos, founder & creative director, Mark Studios LLC Ask for Help Before Depletion The decision I see high performers regret most isn’t burning out. It’s waiting until they’re depleted to ask for help, because by then the choice is already gone. Their body makes it for them. I’m a licensed counselor supervisor and president of a South Carolina practice with more than 60 therapists across 10 offices, plus online therapy. I watch this play out in my own field constantly. The strongest clinicians I supervise are usually the last ones to bring a hard case to supervision. Asking feels like admitting they can’t handle it, and they’ve built their whole identity around being the person others lean on. So they carry it quietly. And it doesn’t show up right away. It shows up months later as irritability, or dread on Sunday nights, or a sudden wish to quit work they used to love. What I tell them is pretty straightforward. Build the support in while things are still going well. Put a standing check-in on the calendar with a supervisor, a mentor, or a therapist before there’s anything urgent to report. When I started my practice with my husband, David, in 2019, I learned fast that the same logic applies to running a company. Support that you set up early costs you maybe an hour a week. Support that you set up late costs you a year of recovery. The best time to ask for help is when you don’t feel like you need it yet. Kenza Haddock, president, Oceanic Counseling Group Broadcast Accomplishments to Gain Advocacy High performers are great at getting things done, often to the detriment of their career progression. If you’re so busy taking care of things, then communicating out what you’re accomplishing is often the last thing on your list. That’s either because you don’t want to brag, or you assume others know what you’re working on. Not learning to communicate up and out is often a regret. I’ve worked with a senior leader whose manager was let go. They established relationships with their upcoming manager and also with other senior leaders in the organization. They learned to communicate regularly as a part of their role to inform the what and the why of their accomplishments through one reorg after another. When yet another manager was let go, they were promoted into the role due to the awareness and extended support they’d built. I’m now working with a younger employee with a new manager on how to own their weekly reporting, proactively communicating to the team what their weekly accomplishments are and how these fit into the greater goals. People can only advocate for you if they can say what you actually do. High performers often learn this alternate side of their role far too late. Dana Zellers, executive & leadership coach, team facilitator, Dana Zellers Own Your Professional Future I’ve talked with more than a thousand executives in the past four years and the biggest regrets that I hear from high performers is relying on their employers to take care of them instead of taking ownership for their career decisions. I have had more clients than I can count who worked for Fortune 100 employers for 20+ years. They believed that they would retire with that company, but then the business changed, they lost their job, and they were left trying to figure out where to go next. No matter where you are in your career, you need to remember that companies are usually going to look out for themselves first. You need to plan your career accordingly. “Job hugging” has been the newest trend, where workers hang on to jobs that they don’t necessarily love. Sure, there is risk in leaving your job, but there is also risk at staying in your current job, especially if layoffs are on the horizon. Staying open to potential opportunities, both actively through networking and passively through an optimized LinkedIn profile, is key to building a career that lasts. Colleen Paulson, executive career consultant, Ageless Careers Align Ambition With Desired Work One decision high performers often make too late is to actively manage their careers rather than assuming that success in their current jobs will take care of that for them. Excelling at your job and managing your career are related, but they’re not the same thing. I’ve seen this play out in two ways. First, high performers become exceptionally good at identifying what it takes to succeed within their organizations. They earn promotions, navigate politics, and build expertise and relationships. But they don’t always stop to ask whether what they’re building is what they actually want. Over the last few years, I’ve worked with leaders who realized that the roles they’d spent years working toward had taken them further away from the work they loved, whether that’s working directly with clients or coaching their teams. We often think about the title and impact, but not the altitude we’ll have to lead at. A promotion often means moving away from doing the work yourself to creating the conditions for others to do it, through strategy, resource allocation, and management. That’s a very different job. Second, high performers forget to build career optionality before they need it. They invest heavily in building skills, relationships, and credibility within their organizations. That’s important, but incomplete. Internal recognition matters, but so does building an external professional network. Think of it as a savings account you’re contributing to over time. Too often, I’ve coached leaders who gave everything to their organizations, sometimes staying for more than a decade, only to find themselves facing a layoff, burnout, or a desire to pivot—and realizing they had limited external networks and little understanding of how their skills would translate elsewhere. A few simple ways to avoid these traps: • Before pursuing a promotion, talk to people already in the role. Understand what their day-to-day looks like, what they’ve had to give up, and what success actually requires. • While you’re happily employed, invest in relationships outside your organization and learn about other industries. Volunteer opportunities and nonprofit board service can be excellent ways to do this while also giving back. • The goal is not to constantly be on a job hunt. It’s to make sure you’re building a career that reflects what you want, with the flexibility to make different choices along the way. Lisa Friscia, president and founder, Franca Consulting Pursue Ventures Through Small Bets One decision high performers often regret making too late is waiting to act on an entrepreneurial idea because it feels safer to stay on secure footing. With more responsibility, high performers can get attached to income or get sucked into “golden handcuffs.” They’re less likely to leave for a more enjoyable job or take a risk at starting something up. I have seen this with seasoned corporate leaders who had a viable concept for years, but once they were settled with a mortgage, family responsibilities, and a stable role, the leap started to feel like too much to lose. The regret often sharpens when they later watch someone else succeed with a similar idea, because possibility suddenly looks like proof that they could have moved earlier. What could have been done differently is keeping the risk muscle active through small, regular bets while still employed, such as testing the idea in low-stakes ways and building comfort with uncertainty. That approach reduces the gap between the idea and bringing it to market, so the decision is not one big, intimidating jump. Also, it’s important to have accountability partners who ask us hard questions or challenge the status quo related to our experience, comfort, and career. How much money is enough? When is the right time? I hear high performers regret missed opportunities with a radical role departure or a job abroad or starting something new, going back to school when they were younger. We feel guilted or bullied into the norm by our families, peers, neighbors and society to do the “right” and “responsible” thing, then later wish we had taken the road less traveled or taken a risk. Janice Perkins, executive coach, Janice Perkins Restore Health Through Daily Habits The one decision high performers often regret is not focusing on their health and well-being as a function of improving their daily performance. All too often, high performers have had success all of their lives. They create habits in their 20s when their energy levels are high and their body can bounce back relatively rapidly. As they start to advance their career in their 30s, 40s, and 50s, these high performers continue with these same habits, focusing only on work. Working late, missing sleep, skipping meals, and perhaps drinking alcohol (even in moderate amounts) drain more and more energy, physical and mental, from their daily output. To these habits, they add coffee to wake up and sugar intake to combat the energy crashes. This leads to poor sleep, and the cycle continues every day. It is possible to reverse these bad habits with small intentional changes in one’s daily lifestyle. A couple of simple examples are arising at the same time every day, including weekends, and getting morning daylight within the first 60-120 minutes of waking up. Steve Fiore, executive performance advisor, Rooted in Curiosity Serve Your Network Regularly As a career coach, I usually connect with high performers when they are in the midst of, or planning for, a transition. The #1 regret I hear is that leaders feel they lost touch with their network while building their careers. They understandably hesitate to make an ask when they haven’t connected in three, five, or even 10+ years. It can feel cringey and awkward reaching out when so much time has passed. But now more than ever, your network is your career net worth. So I hope more high achievers keep that in mind. The easiest way to keep in touch with your network? Be a helper. Haley McNeel Drake, résumé writer & career coach, The Career Revisory Exit Places That Diminish Your Worth One important decision I’ve seen time and time again among high performers is not leaving an organization sooner when their value went unrecognized. Being a high performer doesn’t automatically translate to timely promotions or special accolades for great work. In the pursuit of success, a high performer can work to increase their visibility and yet those efforts don’t lead to a promotion. Not because they’re doing anything wrong or focused on things that won’t get them noticed, but because of office politics or favoritism. What people often overlook and hate to admit is that you simply may be in the wrong environment where no matter what you do, your value will be unrecognized. For high performers, staying too long in an environment after making efforts to be “promotion ready” will eventually catch up, once they end up in an environment where they are valued, appreciated, and recognized for their work. Owning your competence, knowing your value, and being honest with yourself is part of high performance. Not getting a promotion the first time you ask for one isn’t necessarily a sign that you need to start looking or you’re being undervalued. However, the challenge arises when the same cycle repeats, and you’re getting empty promises instead of a kept word. Pay attention to nuance, yes: changes in the broader organization, natural attrition, etc. Timing is everything. But also, give yourself a timeline. If the opportunities you want to pursue don’t become available within that timeline, and those in charge can’t give you a blueprint to help you get where you want to be, you then make a different decision. And that could be planning your exit. Lisa De Nicola, leadership & executive coach; founder, HER Lead; Lisa De Nicola Broaden Expertise Outside Familiar Functions One decision high performers often make too late is stepping outside the area where they’ve already proven themselves. When you’re good at something, you tend to get more of it. You get promoted, take on bigger responsibilities, and become the person everyone relies on. That’s great for your career, but it can also keep you in a fairly narrow lane. Earlier in my career at HD Supply, I spent time working directly with branch managers, and one thing I did was lead financial literacy sessions. These were for people making decisions every day about pricing, inventory, customers, and how to run their businesses. I learned a tremendous amount from those conversations. They helped me understand the operating decisions behind the financial results, and that made me a much better finance leader. Looking back, I would have sought out more of that exposure earlier rather than waiting for opportunities to come through my formal responsibilities. My advice to high performers is to take on something outside your comfort zone before you feel completely ready. Spend time with customers, get involved in operations, or volunteer for a project that forces you to learn another part of the business. Being really good at your current job gets you noticed. Understanding how the whole business works prepares you for the next one. Thomas DeFabrizio, CFO, Vertage.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

#47014. Latest Update: To win the AI search wars, stop chasing the answers and start shaping the questions

Latest Update: To win the AI search wars, stop chasing the answers and start shaping the questions

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1514 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that AI is changing how people choose between brands.
  • AI is changing how people choose between brands.
  • Personal agents like Meta’s Muse take their cues from things like your email inbox and run with what they find.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that AI is changing how people choose between brands. And it’s moving from answering people’s questions to taking action on their behalf. Personal agents like Meta’s Muse take their cues from things like your email inbox and run with what they find. Now if that sounds scary, you’re behind the curve. More than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada started using Muse in its first six weeks. The number one thing they’re using it for? Shopping. And not just for massive purchases. In a McKinsey survey across 11 markets, nearly one-third (29%) of people who shop with artificial intelligence mentioned it was the strongest influence on their last purchase. Groceries are now the second most common thing people buy directly inside an AI tool, just behind clothes. Availability bias Historically, brands have grown on the back of a human shortcut called availability bias. When it comes to most everyday choices, the average person instinctively reaches for the brand that’s first to mind and first to find. AI behaves differently. It’s more literal than it is lazy, and the same is true whether it’s ChatGPT or a Grok Bot. It favors well-known brands when everything else is equal. In a recent study of AI skincare recommendations, the models picked the well-known brand every time when the products were identical. But give a lesser-known rival a rating that’s even less than a tenth of a star higher, and that stopped. Most of the time AI is prepared to compare, matching what a person wants against what a brand delivers. No wonder then that generative engine optimization (GEO), which means making sure your brand is the answer when someone asks AI, has become big business. And it works. BCG reports that a luxury fashion group fixed the structured data behind its website, and within eight weeks the rate at which AI search linked to its site had more than doubled. The problem is that it mostly works when you’re the only one doing it. In the skincare study, when every brand used the same technique, the gains all but canceled out, and brands that sat it out disappeared from the recommendations. GEO looks destined to become a cost of entry, not an advantage. A better way So, is there a better way? Rather than chasing the answer, what if a brand could shape the question people ask? Every choice has two sides: the person’s criteria and the brand’s attributes. A brand gets chosen when the two line up. GEO is about optimizing how a brand presents its attributes. What I’m suggesting is optimizing the criteria people bring. Marketing has a track record of changing what’s important to people. Brands can make things matter more than they’ve mattered before. Volvo, for example, made safety the way to judge a car. Nike did the same for cushioning in running shoes. Others changed how people judge. Dyson moved vacuums from suction power to suction that lasts. Avis moved car rentals from who’s biggest to who tries hardest. And some gave people something latest to look for, as Head & Shoulders did with dandruff. Better still, frame the question around an attribute only you have. Ask AI for the best phone for FaceTime and there’s only one answer, and 88% of American teenagers already own an iPhone, according to a spring 2025 survey from Piper Sandler, the investment bank. In China, where people choose skincare by ingredient, L’Oréal’s Pro-Xylane became one of the most sought after, and only L’Oréal brands can use the name. Where do you start? Find the attribute you win on, relative to your size, and check that people and AI agree. If they disagree, shaping the question can backfire. If people believe something about your brand and AI doesn’t, you make the question matter and AI recommends a rival. If AI believes something about your brand and people don’t, AI recommends you, but nobody asks. Consider Dr. Whitney Bowe, the New York dermatologist who coined “skin cycling” on TikTok. She gave people a new question to ask, and retailers like Boots published guides on what to buy for it. Then she launched her own brand, with a skin-cycling kit. She shaped the question, then built the brand to answer it. Maybe there are two new questions for every brief from here on out. What attribute do we win on? What question do we want people to ask? Shape the question, and you won’t have to chase the answer.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google Fi Wireless is the latest first-party app to adopt a floating toolbar as part of a small navigation redesign.
  • Previously, the companion app still used a tall Material 3 bottom bar.
  • In a recent development, the tabs remain Home, Strategy, Billing, Shop, and Support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google Fi Wireless is the latest first-party app to adopt a floating toolbar as part of a small navigation redesign.

Previously, the companion app still used a tall Material 3 bottom bar. With the network switching update announced last week, Google Fi now has a floating navigation toolbar.

In a recent development, the tabs remain Home, Strategy, Billing, Shop, and Support. A pill-shaped tab indicator is leveraged, while there’s a prominent shadow effect. Given the floating nature, you see what’s around the toolbar, while Fi Wireless now extends underneath the system navigation bar.

However, the Shop tab loads a webpage as before, resulting in a gap and wasted space.

There’s now a floating action button for the newly introduced Google AI-powered Ask Fi chatbot. It provides “instant account help and troubleshooting.” If you ask for human support, the contents of the conversation carry over.

This redesign is rolling out with version 171 of the app as a server-side upgrade. Google Fi joins Google Photos, Chat, and Pixel Now Playing in adopting floating navigation, which is likely the latest first-party mandate for a more edge-to-edge design.

Industry observers note that secondary network switching is not yet widely available, with Google telling us last week that it’s a gradual rollout. The MVNO is also ending Pixel exclusivity for Wi-Fi Auto Connect+ with availability on “select” Samsung and Motorola phones.

Sporting 19 programmable buttons, this capable wireless mouse is an all-time low. The Naga V2 Hyperspeed usually retails for $99.99 and has now dropped to just $56.99 in this seasonal offer.

Recent findings suggest that gaming mice are typically pretty simple affairs, but an MMO mouse offers you the option to program a side plate with 12 additional buttons to your liking. Using Razer's Synapse software, you can bind almost any key you like, which is not only handy for those going out on raids in World of Warcraft, but also for folks who might be missing a numpad on a tenkeyless keyboard.

In a recent development, the mouse itself sports Razer's own HyperSpeed wireless tech and its Focus Pro 30K Optical sensor, meaning that it's built for cord-free gaming. With battery life cited at running over 400 hours over Bluetooth, or 25 hours over 2.4Ghz, you won't be left out of the action for long. You also get Razer's tactile Hyperscroll tech on the wheel, which can flip between smooth and tactile at will.

The Razer Naga V2 Hyperspeed offers 19 programmable buttons, a Focus Pro 30K optical sensor, the tech giant's Gen 2 mechanical mouse switches, and boasts 250 hours of battery life using its included HyperSpeed dongle, or 400 hours over Bluetooth.

If you're keen on something a little higher-end and versatile, then you can still find a solid price on Razer's Naga V2 Pro gaming mouse, which is 28% off at Amazon. The difference between the two models is that the V2 Pro sports a customizable side plate, where you can switch between the 12-button, 6-button, and 2-button side plates using a magnetic connector, making it adaptable for any gaming scenario. You also get upgraded optical Gen 3 switches, a more customizable mouse wheel, and compatibility with Razer's Mouse Dock Pro for wireless charging.

While it's since been supplanted by the Razer Naga V3 Pro, the Naga V2 Pro still has chops in every area that counts, something that our review calls "an excellent all-around performer".

The Razer Naga V2 Pro sports a customizable magnetic side plate, offering 12-, 6-, and 2-button configurations, Razer's Hyperscroll Pro wheel, fully wireless connectivity, and its Focus Pro 30K Optical sensor.

While both of these mice have been out on the market for a while, this is the best prices that we've seen on each of them thus far. If you want to shell out for the newer models, which offer a marginal upgrade over the V2, you'll have to spend $179.99. Comparatively speaking, under $60 and under $150 make both options incredibly attractive.

Both mice are crammed with features that are unlocked by Razer's Synapse software, which allows you to get the most out of the mouse by programming its side plate to your liking, making it excellent for both productivity and gaming.
