📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if you're looking for a new mechanical keyboard on this side of Black Friday, look no further than the Asus ROG Strix Scope II 96 Wireless. The capable gaming keyboard has hit an all-time low price, reducing the board from its original price of $179.99 to just $109.99 at Amazon. Sporting premium build quality, a rotary wheel, and much more, this feature-packed board is crammed with premium touches you won't find on other modern gaming keyboards.

According to recent reports, the Asus ROG Strix Scope II 96 Wireless features a black metal top plate, double-shot PBT keycaps with shine-through legends, per-key RGB lighting, Asus' linear ROG NX Snow Switches, sound-dampening foam, a wrist rest, and tri-mode wireless functionality. You can expect battery life on the board to range from 90 hours with the lights on, all the way to a rated 1,500 hours with it all turned off, and over Bluetooth.

The keyboard is packed with premium finishes all over, which makes it feel more like an enthusiast's mechanical keyboard, offering a premium typing experience when compared to many of its peers in the market.

This 96-percent keyboard features a hot-swappable PCB, a three-way knob and a multifunction button for media controls, and comes with a perfectly sized wrist-rest. It also sounds great, thanks to sound-dampening foam in the case.

In our review of the ROG Strix Scope II 96 Wireless, we gave the board a 4.5-star rating, calling the tenkeyless layout a "perfect compromise between gaming/enthusiast and full-size/compact" keyboards. While you'll find linear switches instead of optical, they're fully lubed out of the box, adding to the overall high-quality out-of-the-box experience you typically only get with more enthusiast-focused keyboards. You can also use Asus' Armory Crate software to customize secondary functions, program macros, and create a custom profile for the rotary wheel included on the board, allowing you to program it like any other key.

For those looking to grab a premium mechanical keyboard on the cheap, the ROG Strix Scope II 96 strikes a fine balance between features, size, build quality, and more, offering a cohesive typing and gaming experience that's adaptable to almost any kind of user out there. While Asus' ROG products are often over the top in design, this board is delightfully muted by comparison, and won't look out of place on your desk or in an office. Now hitting an all-time low price point, you're getting a lot for your money here, as the keyboard ships with just about every user out there. For those looking for a smart, no-frills mechanical keyboard this Black Friday, it's hard to go wrong with the ROG Strix Scope II 96 Wireless.

Motorola’s Razr Flex has leaked in full, with the iPhone Duo competitor showing off its wide form factor in two colors, and it looks great.

Following a leaker earlier this morning, SammyGuru has published new images of the Razr Flex, an iPhone Duo and Galaxy Z Fold 8 competitor that Motorola has been teasing for months now.

It has been revealed that these images show the “Dark Botanical Garden” green and “Coriander” brown with woven and leather-like backplates, two rear-facing cameras, and selfie cameras on both displays. The outer display, said to be 4.97 inches, is wide but very compact, while the inner display is wide in the same way that the iPhone Duo is. The inner panel is expected to be around 7 inches in size.

SammyGuru mentions that the hinge can hold itself half-open and that the price might come in at around $1,799 – though any guesses here are up in the air in the age of RAMageddon.

Motorola Razr Flex is expected to launch in early 2027, with CES in January being a very likely launch timeline for the new foldable.

Getting a good deal on storage is difficult, as NAND prices have skyrocketed over the past twelve months and change. Luckily, this offer on a SanDisk 512GB MicroSD Express Card, which is now 24% off at Amazon, is the perfect opportunity to upgrade your storage. Compatible with the Nintendo Switch 2, the MicroSD Express standard is fairly upcoming, making this a great deal for those seeking to upgrade their storage on Nintendo's latest console. At just $98 in this early Amazon Black Friday deal, the card has fallen well below its original list price, making it a shoo-in for an offer you should snap up before it's too late.

This MicroSD Express card is fully certified to work with the Nintendo Switch 2, and older, non-Express MicroSDs won't work in the console. The card uses a PCIe interface and NVMe protocol to deliver stellar read speeds of up to 650 MB/s and write speeds of up to 220 MB/s, which is much quicker than the MicroSDs of yore. We've even listed it as one of the best MicroSD Express cards you can buy for the Switch 2.

In a recent development, with the holiday season coming up, this is the perfect time to fill up your console's storage with newly introduced games, especially as the Switch 2's Game Key Cards require you to download content onto the console, despite coming on a cartridge. With games like Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 demanding up to 86 GB of space, you'll need all the room you can get to keep yourself entertained.

The SanDisk 512 GB MicroSD Express card works with Nintendo Switch 2 and uses the PCIe and NVMe interfaces to reach speeds of up to 650 MB/s and write speeds of up to 220 MB/s.

It's a safe bet to assume that this MicroSD Express card matches the performance of similar MicroSD Express cards from SanDisk at the same capacity. In our extensive testing of the best MicroSD Express cards, you'll see that SanDisk's 512GB offering comes in at the upper echelons of the list. So, whether you're waiting around for a game to transfer or looking to get rapid loading times, SanDisk's 512GB MicroSD Express card performs incredibly well and could save you a precious bit of time over the holiday season.

The MicroSD Express standard is fairly new. Because of this, the heightened prices of NAND mean that typical prices for cards such as these have remained high. Now, with this early Black Friday offer coming in right before Thanksgiving, you can grab this card, download an enormous number of games, and play them while you're out and about, without having to wait to re-download things or delete older games to make room for something else. Just remember, if you're using a Game Key Card on the console, you'll still have to download the game itself, so don't get caught out without ample storage on your console. This deal is one of the best we've seen for a card of this kind, so don't let it pass you by.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

In a recent development, 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

According to recent reports, picking an ecommerce platform is really a decision about which layers you want to own: the storefront, the catalog and order logic, the payment flow, and the hosting underneath. Every platform below draws that line in a different place. If you have already settled the front-end question with a comparison like SitePoint's Astro vs Next.js guide, the next question is what sits behind it. Prices are from each vendor's pricing page as of November 2026.

It has been revealed that shopify is the fully managed option. Basic costs $29 a month with card rates from 2.9% plus 30 cents, and a 2% fee applies to orders processed through a third-party gateway on that strategy. Developers get two routes: Liquid themes, or Hydrogen, Shopify's headless toolkit, where your framework owns routing and rendering and Hydrogen supplies the Storefront API client and cart. Templates exist for React Router on Oxygen and for Next.js on Vercel. Plus starts at $2,300 a month.

In a recent development, whop is a business platform for taking payments and sending payouts, and it sits under a storefront you have already built rather than replacing it. The Checkout element runs in the browser with no server code and no API key on the page. You pass your own order ID as metadata, Whop copies it onto the payment, and your server fulfills from a signed webhook that follows the Standard Webhooks spec. Domestic cards cost 2.7% plus 30 cents with no monthly fee, buyers see payment methods chosen by their location across 195 countries, and the same balance pays out in over 200 countries, including to affiliates or sellers you onboard. Whop's own guide reveals how to integrate a checkout API into a Next.js storefront end to end. The trade-off is that there is no catalog or shipping engine; you collect address fields at checkout and trigger fulfillment from the webhook.

It has been revealed that wooCommerce is a free plugin on WordPress you host yourself, so you own updates, security, and performance. Its payment gateway, WooPayments, charges US merchants 2.9% plus 30 cents per card transaction, 1.5% more for international cards, 2% for currency conversion, and $25 per dispute. Everything is PHP hooks and filters, which makes it the natural pick for agencies already living in WordPress and the wrong pick for anyone who does not want to run a server.

BigCommerce hosts the back end and lets you bring any front end. Core is $29 a month billed annually, capped at $30,000 in trailing annual sales, and plans auto-upgrade as volume grows. There are no platform fees when you use an embedded payment provider, and a 2% fee on Core if you use another one. Catalyst, its reference storefront, is built on Next.js, React Server Components, and the Storefront GraphQL API, and deploys to Vercel.

Medusa is an open-source commerce framework in Node.js and TypeScript, with an MIT-licensed core and a commercial enterprise edition. SitePoint covered it when it was still a young Shopify alternative; it now has over 37,000 GitHub stars. Self-hosting is free. Medusa Cloud starts at $29 a month for development, $99 for launch, and $299 for scale, with no percentage of sales, and the organization claims you can export your data and self-host at any point.

Saleor is a GraphQL-native, API-only commerce platform written in Python and released under the BSD-3 license. Self-hosting is free. Saleor Cloud starts at $1,599 a month for up to $200,000 in monthly sales, with 0.8% on orders above that, and $3,999 a month at the next tier. It is built for teams with a dedicated engineering function and a large catalog, which is exactly who should pay that price.

Own only the storefront, and Shopify or BigCommerce will carry the rest. Own everything, and Medusa or Saleor give you a back end you can read. Already on WordPress, and WooCommerce is the obvious fit. Already have a storefront in Next.js or Astro and only need the money to move, and Whop is the shortest path. Whichever you pick, the checkout is where disputes start, so log what SitePoint's friendly fraud guide for developers recommends from day one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that hardware hacker BigCrimping (Crimp) has made a dedicated portable Wi-Fi NAS that allows for easily reading and copying 3.5" floppy disks over a network. The renaissance of vintage hardware also extends to some early digital cameras, like the Sony Mavica and Panasonic PV-SD families. These point-and-shooters were popular due to using bog-standard 3.5" floppies in PC format. Many folks may still have floppies from this era around, or simply want to breathe newly introduced life into their cameras.

In a recent development, the fresh device is called floppy3.5, and its design is completely open-source. Making one ought to be pretty easy, as Crimp made all the required files available on GitHub, including data for 3D printing the enclosure, and a custom PCB with an RP2354A microcontroller and an ESP32-S3 bridge. Besides those items, you'll need predictable necessities like a battery, a slimline floppy drive, a Wi-Fi module, and a microSD slot.

The onboard monochrome LCD display looks pretty handy, as Crimp made it show a bevy of information, including sector and cylinder counts, a good/bad sector map, file counts, and even a firmware update progress counter. The onboard buttons do what they say: READ to scan the files, or SAVE to dump them to an SD card. The DISP and POWER buttons return you to the home screen, and power the device off and on.

It has been revealed that the card in said slot optionally stores the disk's files, allowing you to easily go around a storeroom or attic and just insert floppies one after another for archival without needing a computer. When it's time to manage content, you can access the floppy3.5's web interface over the network, and even connect to it directly with a USB cable if you need fancier features like fetching entire disk images.

Crimp chose to use the Greaseweazle floppy drive comms protocol instead of relying on a conventional floppy drive controller. Besides saving on hardware, this allows full control over the drive, as Greaseweazle manages a drive's wire signals directly, making for easy imaging and all sorts of direct data manipulation, regardless of a disk's underlying format. By default, floppy3.5 understands FAT12 for its main purpose, but you can use the Greaseweazle utilities over the cable if needed.

There’s a familiar interruption that comes with shopping online: you’ve found what you want, you’re ready to check out, and the store asks you to sign in. Was this the account with your usual password? Did you change it last time? Is it easier to reset it again?

For Black Friday, Proton Pass Plus and Pass Family are both 60% off their regular monthly pricing with a one-year subscription, while Proton Unlimited is 50% off. Pass Plus starts at $1.99 per month, billed annually, making this a good opportunity to get your passwords — and a few other crucial parts of your digital life — organized.

The problem with strong passwords isn’t understanding why you need them; it’s keeping track of a different one for every account.

That’s useful whether you’re creating an account for a single purchase or signing into a service you use every day.

Sources indicate that unique passwords also help limit the fallout from a data breach. If a retailer exposes your login credentials, using a different password elsewhere means those same credentials won’t unlock your other accounts.

With unlimited logins and encrypted vaults that sync across devices, Proton Pass lets you keep those details together as you move between your phone and computer.

Proton Pass is available for practically every platform, from Chrome and Firefox on the web to native macOS, Windows, and Linux apps to, of course, iOS and Android. This makes it trivially easy to access your passwords, passkeys, and API credentials wherever you find yourself.

Black Friday shopping often leaves something behind long after the packages arrive: a steady stream of promotional emails from stores you barely remember visiting.

Proton Pass includes unlimited hide-my-email aliases, giving you an alternative to handing out your real address every time you create an account.

An alias is an extra email address that forwards messages to your normal inbox. You can give it to a shopping website and still receive your order confirmations and delivery updates, without sharing the underlying address you use for everything else.

It has been revealed that if that alias starts receiving spam, you can switch it off. Your real email address stays the same, and you don’t have to update all your other accounts.

According to recent reports, it’s a practical way to put some distance between your primary inbox and the websites you’re trying for the first time. A separate alias for each service also gives you more control: you can stop messages arriving through one address without disrupting the others.

Passwords are only part of what’s worth keeping in a secure, accessible place.

Proton Pass also stores notes, credit card details, and other confidential information in end-to-end encrypted vaults. That makes it useful for the small, everyday moments when you need something sensitive and don’t want to go looking for it.

When you’re booking a flight, saved passport details let you look up the information you need without digging through a drawer halfway through the reservation.

When you’re shopping online, saved card details mean you don’t have to leave the checkout page to find your wallet.

Industry observers note that when you’re traveling, keeping a digital copy of an crucial document within reach gives you a convenient reference while you’re away from home. It doesn’t replace an original document where one is required, but it can save you from searching through scattered files and messages.

In a recent development, pass Plus also includes a built-in two-factor authenticator, Dark Web Monitoring, and secure link and vault sharing. Those features give you more ways to manage access to your accounts and share sensitive information when you need to.

Pass Plus is the straightforward choice for one person who wants password generation, autofill, unlimited aliases, and secure storage.

Pass Family includes six Pass Plus accounts and a family admin panel. If several people in your household need a password manager, it’s worth considering rather than setting everyone up with separate subscriptions.

Proton Unlimited bundles Pass with Proton VPN, Proton Mail, Proton Drive, and more, including 500 GB of cloud storage. It’s the option to consider if you also want a VPN, encrypted email, and cloud storage alongside your password manager.

A password manager isn’t the most conspicuous Black Friday purchase, but it’s one you can put to work immediately: the next account you create, the next password you forget, or the next time a checkout asks for details you don’t have handy.

I’ve been using a Keychron Q3 HE for quite some time now. Over the last year or two, I’ve made a lateral move to Gateron Dawn double-rail magnetic switches from the stock Nebula switches it came with. Now, Keychron sells a Q3 HE with improved hardware for an 8K polling rate and with Lime silent switches by default.

It’s an excellent keyboard, and my only complaint is that the white variant I have doesn’t exactly match my desk.

Industry observers note that most of Keychron’s deals are good right now, but the standout is the Thunderbolt 5 Dock, which was released earlier this year. I have mine plugged into my Mac Mini for the time being, but I use it on my Windows PC and Googlebook without problem. The Thunderbolt 5 rating means it keeps up with next-gen speeds, but it’s backward-compatible and works with most devices. Just plug in a host device, and you have access to data and displays easily.

In a recent development, the Keychron Thunderbolt 5 Dock is down to $314, instead of $349. Considering it just launched earlier in the year, now is a good time to get one if you’re looking for a docking option.

Right now, Keychron has a number of deals running that are worth checking out.

The 8K Q3 HE magnetic keyboard from Keychron is down to $206 at 10% off. It was already a great deal for a fully aluminum case with good keycaps and excellent switches, but the newly introduced Black Friday deal sweetens the pot a little.

In a recent development, the classic Q3 HE is no slouch, though. I’d recommend it in an instant, and it’s down to $191 instead of $239. That’s $48 down from the traditional price, and a much better deal than the 8K version if you don’t absolutely need the insanely high polling rate.

The K4 HE is another great option, and it’s a much friendlier $81 on Amazon. That’s down from the $115 it normally is. It’s another hall-effect (magnetic switch) keyboard, but with wood accents and in a smaller 60% layout.

Keychron’s deals won’t last into next month, ending on November 30.
